PM2E-CH-FINAL-002.q: An oil-price shock lowers real output while raising inflation and unemployment. Why is this a harder stabilization problem than an ordinary demand-side recession?
options: Supporting output can worsen inflation, while restraining inflation can deepen the output and unemployment loss.
Supporting output can reduce unemployment, but because inflation originated from aggregate demand, inflation will necessarily fall as output recovers.
Demand restraint can lower inflation without an additional output cost because the original loss of output came from supply.
Because inflation and unemployment rise together, policymakers can stabilize both by returning aggregate demand to its original level.
PM2E-CH-FINAL-002.feedback: An adverse supply shock raises inflation while reducing output and employment. Supporting demand can limit the output loss but add inflation pressure; restraining demand can reduce inflation pressure but deepen the output loss. The fact that the original shock came from supply does not remove the output cost of demand restraint.

LG-Q-358.q: Money demand increases while the money supply remains fixed. What is the likely effect on the interest rate and interest-sensitive investment?

r rises and investment rises.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-139.q: A higher price level raises money demand and the interest rate, reducing investment. Which feature of aggregate demand does this explain?

P52A-AD-B1-001.q: Consumer spending plans rise $20 at every price level while an unexpected rise in the price level changes the quantity demanded along AD. How does each change affect the AD curve?
options: Spending plans shift AD right; the price-level rise moves upward along an AD curve
Spending plans move upward along AD; the price-level rise shifts AD right
Both events shift AD right because both involve nominal expenditure
Both events move along AD because no supply condition changed
P52A-AD-B1-001.feedback: A non-price spending change shifts the schedule. The price level is an axis variable, so its change is represented as movement along a given schedule, holding its other determinants fixed.

P52A-AD-B2-002.q: Consumer spending plans rise $60 at every price level while an unexpected rise in the price level changes the quantity demanded along AD. How does each change affect the AD curve?
options: Both events shift AD right because both involve nominal expenditure
Both events move along AD because no supply condition changed
Spending plans shift AD right; the price-level rise moves upward along an AD curve
Spending plans move upward along AD; the price-level rise shifts AD right
P52A-AD-B2-002.feedback: A non-price spending change shifts the schedule. The price level is an axis variable, so its change is represented as movement along a given schedule, holding its other determinants fixed.

P52A-AD-LB-003.q: Consumer spending plans rise by $100 at every price level. An unexpected price-level increase then leaves the observed quantity of output demanded unchanged. Does the unchanged quantity mean aggregate demand did not shift?
options: Yes. An unchanged observed quantity proves that spending plans did not change at any price level.
No. The higher price itself shifted AD left, while higher spending caused movement along the old curve.
Yes. Price-level changes and spending-plan changes are both movements along one unchanged AD curve.
No. AD shifted right, but movement along the new curve at the higher price offset the increase in observed quantity.
P52A-AD-LB-003.feedback: The $100 fixed-price spending increase is an AD shift. A higher price lowers quantity demanded along the new curve. An unchanged final quantity can conceal both changes; it does not establish an unchanged demand schedule.

P52A-AD-B1-003.q: A country initially sells $40 of exports. Foreign income rises while domestic business confidence falls. No magnitudes are given. What can be concluded about aggregate demand when both changes occur?
options: Exports and investment both tend to fall; AD shifts left
Exports tend to rise and investment to fall; opposite signs establish exactly unchanged AD
Exports tend to rise and investment to fall; the net AD direction is uncertain
Exports and investment both tend to rise; AD shifts right
P52A-AD-B1-003.feedback: Foreign demand supports exports while weaker confidence reduces investment. Competing components require relative magnitudes before assigning a net AD shift.

P52A-AD-B3-003.q: A country initially sells $80 of exports. Foreign income rises while domestic business confidence falls. No magnitudes are given. What can be concluded about aggregate demand when both changes occur?

LG-Q-2007.q: A bank has deposits of $1000, reserves of $200, and a required reserve ratio of 10% in a simplified model. A depositor withdraws $100 in currency. Assume no other balance-sheet change. How does the withdrawal affect required and excess reserves?
options: Reserves become $100, required reserves become $110, and there is a $10 shortfall
Reserves become $100, required reserves $90, and excess reserves $10
Reserves become $100, required reserves remain $100, and excess reserves are zero
Reserves stay $200, required reserves become $90, and excess reserves $110
LG-Q-2007.feedback: The cash withdrawal reduces deposits and reserves by 100. Required reserves are 10% of 900 = 90; actual reserves 100 leave 10 excess. Both sides of the reserve calculation must reflect the withdrawal.

P52A-BANK-B2-003.q: A bank has deposits of $1800, reserves of $360, and a required reserve ratio of 10% in a simplified model. A depositor withdraws $180 in currency. Assume no other balance-sheet change. How does the withdrawal affect required and excess reserves?
options: Reserves stay $360, required reserves become $162, and excess reserves $198
Reserves become $180, required reserves become $198, and there is a $18 shortfall
Reserves become $180, required reserves $162, and excess reserves $18
Reserves become $180, required reserves remain $180, and excess reserves are zero
P52A-BANK-B2-003.feedback: The cash withdrawal reduces deposits and reserves by 180. Required reserves are 10% of 1620 = 162; actual reserves 180 leave 18 excess. Both sides of the reserve calculation must reflect the withdrawal.

P52A-BANK-B2-001.q: A bank has reserves of $320 and deposits of $1600; the simplified required reserve ratio is 10%. Management says it can lend all $320 without acquiring reserves. Which correction is justified before considering capital and credit risk?
options: Only $160 is initially excess reserves; the $160 required portion must remain against existing deposits
All $320 is excess because required reserves are calculated only after lending
No reserves are excess because every reserve dollar is bank capital
It can lend $3200 immediately from its own reserves because the system multiplier applies to one bank's first loan
P52A-BANK-B2-001.feedback: Required reserves are .10×1600 = 160; excess is 320−160 = 160. A single bank's immediate capacity is distinct from a system-wide redepositing maximum.

P52A-BANK-B3-001.q: A bank has assets of $2400, deposit liabilities of $2000 and capital of $400. Loan losses reduce assets by $600; liabilities do not fall. Which remedy addresses the resulting problem?
options: Capital: +$400; loan losses affect liquidity rather than the owners' residual claim.
Capital: +$1000; writing off loans reduces deposit liabilities rather than bank assets.
Capital: $0 after borrowing $200; the loan raises assets without matching liabilities.
Capital: −$200; new equity addresses insolvency, a liquidity loan alone does not.
P52A-BANK-B3-001.feedback: After losses, assets are 1800 and liabilities 2000; capital is −200. Borrowed liquidity raises assets and liabilities equally, leaving net worth unchanged.

LG-Q-9104.q: A bank has assets of $1440, deposit liabilities of $1200 and capital of $240. Loan losses reduce assets by $360; liabilities do not fall. Which remedy addresses the resulting problem?
options: Capital: −$120; new equity addresses insolvency, a liquidity loan alone does not.
Capital: +$240; loan losses affect liquidity rather than the owners' residual claim.
Capital: +$600; writing off loans reduces deposit liabilities rather than bank assets.
Capital: $0 after borrowing $120; the loan raises assets without matching liabilities.
LG-Q-9104.feedback: After losses, assets are 1080 and liabilities 1200; capital is −120. Borrowed liquidity raises assets and liabilities equally, leaving net worth unchanged.

LG-Q-2011.q: In a simplified reserve-ratio exercise, a bank has deposits of $1400 and reserves of $280. The required ratio rises from 10% to 15%, with balances otherwise unchanged. Which result and limitation are correct?
options: Excess reserves: $140→$70; actual lending must fall by exactly $70.
Excess reserves: $140→$210; the higher ratio releases $70 for additional lending.
Excess reserves: $140→$70; actual lending also depends on bank and borrower responses.
Capital: $140→$70; the higher reserve requirement writes down assets by $70.
LG-Q-2011.feedback: Old required reserves=140; new required reserves=.15×1400=210. Excess falls from 140 to 70. Balance-sheet capacity is not a complete behavioral lending forecast.

P52B-S3-MPT-B3-001.q: In a simplified reserve-ratio exercise, a bank has deposits of $3000 and reserves of $600. The required ratio rises from 10% to 15%, with balances otherwise unchanged. Which result and limitation are correct?

LG-Q-9113.q: In a simplified reserve-ratio exercise, a bank has deposits of $2,200 and reserves of $440. The requirement rises from 10% to 15%, with balances unchanged. The bank was already unwilling to lend because no applicant met its credit standards. Does the reserve change establish a $110 reduction in actual lending?
options: No. Excess reserves fall from $220 to $110, but credit standards were already binding; reserve capacity alone does not determine actual lending.
Yes. Every dollar decline in excess reserves must remove a dollar of loans regardless of borrower quality.
No. Excess reserves rise to $330 because the larger requirement increases lending capacity.
Yes. The requirement writes down bank capital by $110, forcing the same loan reduction.
LG-Q-9113.feedback: Required reserves rise from 220 to 330, leaving 110 excess. That accounting change does not reveal an actual loan reduction when the bank already rejects applicants. Reserve availability, capital and creditworthiness are distinct constraints.

43100.q: A forecast shows revenues $250, outlays $350, and borrowing $100. A later forecast raises revenues by $50 with outlays fixed. How does the projected deficit change, and does the revision show that debt has already been repaid?
options: The projected deficit falls to $50; this is a revised forecast, not proof actual debt already fell
The projected deficit becomes a $50 surplus; any revenue gain eliminates all borrowing
The projected deficit remains $100; forecasts cannot respond to revenue assumptions
Actual debt immediately falls $50; a forecast revision is a realized repayment
43100.feedback: New projected deficit = 350−300=50. A projection is conditional; it is not a record of completed borrowing or repayment.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9002.q: From AD1-AS2, a supply disruption moves the economy to AS1. Officials then choose AD2 to restore output. If their goal had instead been the original price level, would that same demand response achieve it?
options: No. AD2 restores Y1 but raises prices to P3; the original price target would require demand restraint and a larger output loss.
No. AD2 raises output to Y2 and prices to P2; the original price target would require demand restraint and a larger output loss.
Yes. Returning to Y1 at P3 restores the original price level because productive capacity is unchanged.
Yes. Any demand change that restores potential output also reverses the price effect of a supply disruption.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9002.feedback: The original point is Y1/P1, the supply-shock point Y3/P2, and accommodationY 1/P3. Supporting output worsens the price-level increase. With disrupted supply fixed, bringing prices back down instead requires lower demand and more output loss.

ECON-SP-HARD-214.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy starts at AD1-AS2 and AD shifts to AD2, what gap appears?
options: Inflationary gap
Recessionary gap
No output gap
Supply gap
ECON-SP-HARD-214.feedback: The economy moves to Y2, which is above natural output, so it creates an expansionary gap.

43122.q: Government pays $30 in interest and repays $120 in principal on maturing debt. How much is interest expense, and how should the principal repayment be treated?
options: Interest expense is $30; principal repayment reduces liabilities or is refinanced, rather than becoming interest expense
Interest expense is $150; every cash payment on debt is interest
Interest expense is $120; only the maturing face value measures financing cost
Interest expense is zero if new securities finance the cash payment
43122.feedback: Interest is the cost of borrowing over the period. Principal retires an existing liability; refinancing changes financing flows but does not reclassify principal as interest.

43151.q: How does financing a government deficit through borrowing affect public debt?
options: Borrowing reduces outstanding debt by the amount of the deficit.
Borrowing turns the budget deficit into a surplus without changing debt.
Borrowing raises tax revenue, leaving the outstanding debt unchanged.
Borrowing adds to the outstanding debt used to finance the deficit.
43151.feedback: Borrowing commonly finances a deficit, and repeated borrowing adds to outstanding debt.

43326.q: What does the link between investment and capital formation tell us about productive capacity?
options: It explains every determinant of productivity
It derives a complete production function
It isolates one channel from investment to productive capacity
It proves convergence across all economies
43326.feedback: The relationship isolates how new investment can add to the capital stock; it does not by itself explain every determinant of productivity or growth.

43302.q: A deficit increases by $30 billion while private saving rises by $10 billion. In the loanable-funds model, how does this affect the real interest rate and private investment?

Investment demand shifts right by $30 billion because deficits directly raise project profitability
Supply shifts left, raising the rate and crowding out investment
National saving rises $40 billion, so the real rate falls and private investment expands
43302.feedback: The relevant chain is public saving down, only partly offset by private saving, then national saving and loanable-funds supply down. The task does not calculate short-run aggregate-demand multipliers.

ECON-NL-EASYBOSS-2018.q: A fixed basket costs $140 in the base year, $168 this year and $184.8 next year. A report treats the increase in CPI index points as the inflation rate. What are next year's CPI and inflation rate?

The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 32%
The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 10%
The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 12%

No; prices rise 4%, and real purchasing power falls about 1.0%
Yes; prices rise only 3.8%, which is below the payment rise
Yes; a rising nominal payment guarantees more purchasing power

The rail price rise is entirely a quality change; no pure inflation occurred
The change proves the whole CPI should fall because one alternative is cheaper
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9028.feedback: The same service can be maintained at lower cost by changing an existing bundle, which is the substitution mechanism. A travel example alone does not measure the full index’s bias or imply that overall prices fell.

PM2B2-BIAS-FB-005.q: A product originally costs $230. Its replacement costs 20% more but provides twice the measured service, with no other relevant quality changes. How should the price change be interpreted after allowing for the improved service?

The comparable price is unchanged; a new version is always treated as having the old price.
The price per unit of service falls; counting the entire sticker-price increase as inflation ignores the quality improvement.

LG-Q-2008.q: The public deposits $120 of previously held currency in a system with rr=10%, no later currency leakage and no excess reserves. At the maximum deposit expansion predicted by this model, how does total deposit expansion compare with the net increase in M1?

LG-Q-9109.q: A textbook system has rr=25%, no currency leakage and no excess reserves. Policy removes $160 in reserves. Which statement combines the direction and meaning of the model's maximum adjustment?

LG-R-5013.q: A bank makes a new loan by crediting the borrower’s deposit account. Which statement best describes the textbook balance-sheet effect?

The bank permanently loses required reserves equal to the full loan amount
The bank creates new capital equal to the loan and leaves deposits unchanged
The central bank must approve and create each commercial-bank loan individually
LG-R-5013.feedback: When the bank credits the borrower’s account, it records a loan asset and a matching deposit liability; the bank does not hand over a preexisting pile of reserves.

PM2A-DIS-L-010.q: Inflation falls 3 points while cumulative output loss equals 6% of annual GDP. Unemployment later returns to its natural rate. What is the sacrifice ratio, and is the unemployment increase permanent?
options: The sacrifice ratio is 0.5, and unemployment stays permanently high
The ratio is 3, and LRPC shifts right permanently
The ratio is 6, and the price level must have fallen
The sacrifice ratio is 2, and the unemployment cost was temporary in the model
PM2A-DIS-L-010.feedback: The sacrifice ratio is 6/3=2 percent of annual output per percentage-point inflation reduction. The given return to natural unemployment means the unemployment cost is temporary in this model; disinflation alone need not make the price level fall.

PM2A-DIS-EB-012.q: A credible disinflation announcement lowers expectations before demand falls; contracts can reset immediately. Compare this with identical demand restraint under fixed old expectations.
options: Earlier contract adjustment increases the temporary increase in unemployment by shifting SRPC upward.
Earlier contract adjustment leaves the temporary increase unchanged because expectations do not affect wages.
Earlier contract adjustment permanently lowers natural unemployment despite unchanged labor-market structure.
Earlier contract adjustment can reduce the temporary increase in unemployment for that restraint.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9008.q: Compare disinflations from b to the lower sustained inflation rate in the diagram. Supply conditions and natural unemployment do not change. ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9008.feedback: The plotted disinflation is from b at I2 to c at I1. With old expectations it can pass through d at U3. If expectations and relevant contracts already adjust, the lower SRPC supports c without that initial gap. This conclusion depends on prompt contract adjustment, not credibility alone.

PM2A-DIS-EB-013.q: After disinflation, unemployment returns to its original natural rate and the inflation rate stabilizes at 2%. The price index is now 180, compared with 160 before. Which claim is supported?

The temporary increase in unemployment has ended; the price level remains higher and is still rising.

PM2A-DIS-EB-013.feedback: A successful reduction in positive inflation need not undo earlier price increases. Longer-run labor adjustment and the cumulative price-level path are different outcomes.

PM2A-DIS-LB-018.q: After disinflation, unemployment returns to its original natural rate and inflation stabilizes at 2%. The price index is 260, up from 240 before the policy. An official says the return to natural unemployment proves the policy had no real transition cost. Is that warranted?

PM2A-DIS-LB-018.feedback: The endpoint establishes that excess unemployment has ended, not that its cumulative cost was zero. A positive 2% inflation rate also means the higher price level continues rising; disinflation does not reverse all prior price increases.

PM2A-DIS-LB-020.q: Inflation falls to 1%, unemployment returns to its natural rate and prices remain higher than before. A second disinflation plan would have reached the same endpoint. Can these facts establish which plan imposed less unemployment during the transition?

PM2A-DIS-LB-020.feedback: Lower positive inflation is disinflation, not a falling price level. Returning to the natural rate ends current excess unemployment, but comparing transition costs requires information about its size and duration along each path.

ECON-SP-MONETARY-POLICY-PC-TRANSITION-60.q: Expected inflation falls and the economy later returns to natural unemployment. How do the short-run and long-run Phillips curves explain this adjustment?

Lower frictional unemployment must raise cyclical unemployment
The natural rate is fixed and cannot respond to matching
Only the measured CPI can change from better matching
PM2B4-LMI-BR-001.feedback: Faster matching reduces frictional unemployment; because frictional unemployment is part of the natural rate, the natural rate can fall.

LG-Q-4001.q: Income rises while the price level falls in an economy with nominal money supply fixed. Which additional evidence is needed to determine whether the interest rate rises or falls?

Prices alone: lower prices pull rates down, income does not affect money demand.

PM2C3-LPMM-BR-001.q: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed, raising the equilibrium interest rate. How does the higher interest rate affect investment and aggregate demand?

The higher interest rate directly increases government purchases.
Aggregate demand is unaffected because interest rates matter only inside the money-market graph.
PM2C3-LPMM-BR-001.feedback: After solving the money market, use the interest-rate change to infer the direction of investment and other rate-sensitive spending, then the aggregate-demand shift.

ECON-NL-RULE-OF-70-5032.q: What can the Rule of 70 estimate?

The unemployment rate

ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-LRAS-6021.q: Technology raises potential output from 100 to 110. If actual output stays 100, what output gap exists relative to the new LRAS?

LG-Q-9024.q: Which statement best combines the simplified deposit-multiplier model with monetary-control limits?

Fractional reserve banking guarantees exact Fed control of M1.
The multiplier works only with commodity money.
Currency drain increases bank reserves and expands lending.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9027.q: A student says nominal wages rose 8 percent, so workers are better off. Inflation was 11 percent. How did workers' real wages change?

Real wages rose because nominal wages increased above zero.
Real wages were unchanged because all inflation is neutral immediately.
Real wages doubled because nominal wages are measured in dollars.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9027.feedback: Real wage growth is approximately nominal wage growth minus inflation, so workers lost purchasing power.

P52B-S3-MPT-B2-001.q: A policy package supplies $240 of reserves but also increases the return banks can earn by holding reserves. What can be concluded about bank lending?
options: Reserve capacity increases, holding reserves becomes more attractive; both changes encourage additional lending equally.
Reserve capacity decreases, holding reserves becomes more attractive; both changes discourage additional lending equally.
Reserve capacity increases, the return on reserves is irrelevant; a fixed multiplier determines lending.
Reserve capacity increases, holding reserves becomes more attractive; the net lending response remains uncertain.

store of value; medium of exchange; unit of account
unit of account; medium of exchange; store of value

PM2B4-NRU-MB-004.q: An economy has frictional unemployment 2%, structural 3% and actual 6%. If a demand recovery removes the cyclical component without changing matching or skills, which rate remains and why?

0%; removing cyclical unemployment also removes frictional and structural components.
3%; frictional unemployment disappears with the cyclical component during recovery.
6%; changes in demand leave all three unemployment components unchanged.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-004.feedback: Natural unemployment=2+3=5; the initial cyclical component is 6−5=1. Recovery alone does not remove search and structural mismatch.

PMOE-POL-EL-002.q: In a short-run comparison before full trade and output adjustment, monetary easing lowers domestic real rates while a foreign recession cuts export demand. Prices are fixed, and NCO is not held fixed across the two shocks. Can the direction of the net change in aggregate demand be determined without knowing the strength of each response?
options: AD falls because foreign income changes exports while monetary policy changes only investment
AD is unchanged because depreciation offsets the export-demand shift one for one
Ambiguous without the relative strengths of higher NX from depreciation and lower export demand
AD rises because the monetary channel determines the exchange rate before exports respond
PMOE-POL-EL-002.feedback: Easing supports domestic investment and, through depreciation, NX. Foreign recession reduces demand for exports. Their short-run AD contributions compete. The fixed-NCO long-run trade-offset result cannot be imposed on this adjustment comparison.

PMOE-POL-L-002.q: In the open-economy loanable-funds model, saving is unchanged and capital flight raises desired NCO $150 billion at the original real interest rate. Final domestic investment falls $110 billion. With net-export demand and price levels fixed, how does the interest-rate response offset the initial capital flight, and what happens to the currency?
options: Feedback raises NCO $40 billion; final NCO rises $190 billion and the currency depreciates
Feedback lowers NCO $110 billion; final NCO rises $40 billion and the currency appreciates
Feedback exactly cancels the shock; NCO and the exchange rate are unchanged
Feedback lowers NCO $40 billion; final NCO rises $110 billion and the currency depreciates
PMOE-POL-L-002.feedback: With ΔS=0 and ΔI=−110, ΔNCO=110. Relative to the initial +150 schedule shift, rate feedback is −40. Final vertical FX supply shifts right by 110, lowering the foreign-currency-per-domestic-currency rate and raising NX.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.q: A firm produces 1100 units at 10 units per labor hour. After training, productivity is 12 units per hour and required output rises to 1320. How many labor hours are needed after both changes?
options: Hours are zero; higher productivity replaces all labor
Hours remain 110; higher output exactly matches the proportional productivity gain
Hours rise to 132; output growth alone sets required hours
Hours fall to 91.7; apply the productivity gain but ignore higher required output
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.feedback: Initial hours = 1100/10 = 110; new hours = 1320/12 = 110. Productivity gains do not necessarily reduce total hours when output demand changes too.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3011.q: A firm produces 1600 units at 10 units per labor hour. After training, productivity is 12 units per hour and required output rises to 1920. How many labor hours are needed after both changes?
options: Hours are zero; higher productivity replaces all labor
Hours remain 160; higher output exactly matches the proportional productivity gain
Hours rise to 192; output growth alone sets required hours
Hours fall to 133.3; apply the productivity gain but ignore higher required output
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3011.feedback: Initial hours = 1600/10 = 160; new hours = 1920/12 = 160. Productivity gains do not necessarily reduce total hours when output demand changes too.

PM2B3-PROD-LB-001.q: A firm produces 2,100 units at 10 units per labor hour. Training raises productivity to 12 units per hour while required output rises to 2,520. Management plans to cut total hours because of the training. Can it meet the new output requirement with fewer hours if no further productivity change occurs?
options: Yes. New required hours are 175 because only the productivity change affects labor needs.
No. Both plans require 210 hours; a cut would require further productivity gains or a lower output target.
No. New required hours are 252 because only output growth affects labor needs.
Yes. A rise in productivity guarantees fewer total hours regardless of the quantity required.
PM2B3-PROD-LB-001.feedback: Initial hours are 2,100/10=210; new hours 2,520/12=210. The proportional output increase uses the full productivity gain. The output requirement is a constraint that prevents cutting hours under unchanged new productivity.

LG-Q-3000.q: The money supply is initially $100, velocity is 4, and real output is 200 units. Money rises 10%, velocity falls 10%, and real output is unchanged. Which conclusion corrects the claim that prices must rise 10%?
options: The price level rises 10%; money growth alone determines prices without a velocity assumption
The price level is unchanged; equal opposite percentage changes exactly cancel
The price level falls 10%; ignore the simultaneous money increase
The price level falls 1%; the opposing percentage changes in M and V combine multiplicatively
LG-Q-3000.feedback: MV=PY. With Y fixed, P changes by the product of M and V factors: 1.10×0.90=.99, a 1% fall. A constant-velocity shortcut is not valid here.

P52B-S4-QTM-B1-001.q: A country has nominal spending $960. It aims for a 3% price-level increase with real output up 2% and velocity down 1%. What money-growth rate is required, and why is adding 3% and 2% incomplete?

Exactly 1% money growth; subtract real growth from the price target
About 6.1% money growth; falling velocity also has to be offset
Exactly 5% money growth; velocity does not affect the target

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3012.q: Use the sum of annual output-gap losses, measured as percentages of the same benchmark annual output of $100. Gaps are −2%, −1%, and −1%; inflation falls from 7% to 5%. An analyst divides by final inflation. Which correction is right?
options: The ratio is 4/5=0.8; divide by the final inflation rate
The ratio is 4/7; divide by the initial inflation rate
The ratio is 1/2=0.5; only the final year's loss matters
The ratio is 4/2=2; divide cumulative loss by the two-point inflation reduction
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3012.feedback: Cumulative loss is 2+1+1=4% of one year's output. The denominator is 7−5=2 percentage points, so the sacrifice ratio is 2, not loss divided by either inflation level.

PM2A-SAC-EB-018.q: Use the sum of annual output-gap losses, measured as percentages of the same benchmark annual output of $180. Gaps are −2%, −1%, and −1%; inflation falls from 7% to 5%. An analyst divides by final inflation. Which correction is right?
options: The ratio is 4/7; divide by the initial inflation rate
The ratio is 1/2=0.5; only the final year's loss matters
The ratio is 4/2=2; divide cumulative loss by the two-point inflation reduction
The ratio is 4/5=0.8; divide by the final inflation rate
PM2A-SAC-EB-018.feedback: Cumulative loss is 2+1+1=4% of one year's output. The denominator is 7−5=2 percentage points, so the sacrifice ratio is 2, not loss divided by either inflation level.

PM2A-SAC-LB-023.q: Annual output gaps are −2%,−1% and−1%, each measured against the same benchmark annual output of $260. Inflation falls 7% to 5%. Officials have a 6% cumulative output-loss budget and expect the observed sacrifice ratio to apply to further disinflation. Does the remaining budget permit lowering inflation to 3%?
options: Yes. Dividing the 4% loss by final inflation 5% gives 0.8, so a further two-point reduction fits.
Yes. Only the final 1% annual gap counts against the budget, leaving 5% for further reduction.
No. All 6% of the budget has already been spent because the initial inflation rate was 7%.
No. The ratio is 2 and only 2% of the loss budget remains, enough for one more inflation point, to 4%.
PM2A-SAC-LB-023.feedback: Cumulative loss is 4% and disinflation 2 points, so the sacrifice ratio is 2. The remaining 2% budget buys one additional point if that ratio continues. A further two-point reduction would require 4% more loss and exceed the stated budget.

PM2A-SAC-LB-024.q: A 3-point disinflation was planned at sacrifice ratio 2, exhausting a 6% loss budget. The first point unexpectedly costs 4%. If remaining disinflation costs 2% per point, how much more disinflation fits the budget, and what would achieving the original target cost?
options: No further point can be achieved because the first loss exceeded its forecast
The target can increase because a larger first loss lowers all later losses mechanically
Only one further point fits the remaining 2% budget; achieving all 3 points would require total loss 8%
All remaining 2 points fit because the original average ratio remains 2 by assumption
PM2A-SAC-LB-024.feedback: The unspent budget is 6−4=2. At 2% per point it buys one further point. Finishing the remaining two would cost 4 more and total 8; the original joint promises are no longer compatible.

43192.q: In an economy with private saving of $150 and public saving of −$30, what is national saving?
43192.feedback: Adding the two components gives national saving of $150 − $30 = $120.

43168.q: A household saves $20 and buys an existing corporate share. A firm separately builds $40 of new domestic equipment. Which purchase counts as investment in GDP, and how can saving help finance it?
options: Both are GDP investment; expected returns make either purchase newly produced capital.
Only shares are GDP investment; saving finances securities while equipment is current consumption.
Shares are financial assets; equipment is GDP investment; saving can finance the latter.
Neither is GDP investment; financing through household saving excludes business capital purchases.
43168.feedback: Saving is income not consumed; buying an existing share changes asset ownership. GDP investment records new capital production. Financial intermediation can connect savers and investors without making the purchases identical.

43177.q: A household saves $100 and buys an existing corporate share. A firm separately produces $200 of new domestic equipment but leaves it in inventory until next year. An analyst counts the share purchase as this year's GDP investment and delays counting the equipment until its sale. What should be corrected?
options: The share is current GDP investment, while unsold equipment cannot enter any current account.
Both should wait until next year because investment requires a household to buy newly produced equipment.
The existing share adds no current production; the new equipment enters this year's inventory investment even before sale.
Both enter this year's GDP investment because every saving transaction creates physical capital.
43177.feedback: Buying an existing share transfers a financial claim. Producing new equipment creates current output, recorded as inventory investment if unsold. A later sale reduces inventory while recording the buyer's acquisition, avoiding counting the same production twice.

P52A-AS-B2-003.q: Firms face higher actual output prices but unchanged expected prices and input costs. An analyst shifts the entire SRAS curve right. Why should this be shown as a movement along SRAS instead?
options: Use a rightward LRAS shift for actual prices; expected prices have no supply implication
Keep output fixed on a vertical SRAS at every horizon because actual prices never affect production
Use movement along SRAS for actual prices; a change in expected prices or input costs would shift the curve
Use a rightward SRAS shift for actual prices; expected prices only move along it
P52A-AS-B2-003.feedback: A schedule relates actual prices and supplied output holding its determinants fixed. Changing that axis variable moves along it; changing expected prices/costs changes the schedule.

LG-R-5056.q: A stimulus is approved during a recession but takes effect only after output has returned close to potential. What risk does the delayed stimulus create?
options: The delayed stimulus can push aggregate demand too far right after the original gap has faded.
The delay automatically turns the stimulus into contractionary policy.
The policy can no longer affect aggregate demand once recovery begins.
The delay directly shifts LRAS left.
LG-R-5056.feedback: A policy can destabilize the economy if it arrives after the original gap has already narrowed or reversed.

LG-R-5058.q: A negative supply shock lowers real output and raises the price level. If policymakers use expansionary demand policy to support output, what tradeoff do policymakers face?
options: It can support output while worsening inflation pressure.
It lowers the price level and raises output with no tradeoff.
It directly shifts SRAS right and restores productive capacity.
It must reduce both output and the price level.
LG-R-5058.feedback: Demand stabilization during a negative supply shock involves a tradeoff: supporting output can worsen price pressure, while reducing inflation can deepen the output loss.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9067.q: A survey begins with 132 employed,12 unemployed and 56 adults outside the labor force. Then 4 unemployed find jobs,3 stop searching,5 adults enter the labor force without finding work, and 2 employed retire. All job seekers are available. Participation ends unchanged. Does that prove nobody entered or left the labor force?
options: No. Five entries offset five exits; participation remains 72% while unemployment falls to about 6.9%.
Yes. An unchanged participation rate means every individual kept the same labor-force status.
No. Participation rises to 75.5% because people who stop searching must remain counted as unemployed.
Yes. Retirements and discouraged exits are ignored in both participation and unemployment statistics.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9067.feedback: Employment becomes 134 and unemployment 10, so the labor force stays 144 of 200. Five entrants offset three search exits and two retirements. An unchanged aggregate participation rate can hide substantial flows; unemployment is 10/144≈6.9%.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9068.q: Among 200 adults, participation is 75% and unemployment 8%. Next month 6 unemployed stop searching,6 employed retire, and 4 adults enter the labor force but find no work. Other statuses are unchanged and seekers are available. A report calls the lower unemployment rate evidence of net job creation. Is that justified?
options: No. Employment falls to 132 even as unemployment drops to about 7.0% and participation to 71%; labor-force exits help explain the lower rate.
Yes. Any lower unemployment rate means the number of employed people increased.
No. Employment stays 138 and participation 75%, because retirees remain employed for this calculation.
Yes. Employment rises to 144 when the four new job seekers and six retirees are added to the initial workforce.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9068.feedback: Initially LF=150, U=12 and E=138. Employment becomes 132; unemployment 12−6+4=10; LF=142. Thus unemployment is about 7.0% and participation 71%. A falling unemployment rate can accompany employment losses when participation also declines.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4039.q: Consider three labor-market observations: a worker is counted as employed even though they want full-time work, another worker is not counted as unemployed because they stopped searching, and actual unemployment is above the natural rate. What do these observations tell us about labor-market conditions?
options: Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural proves only structural unemployment
Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness
Part-time employment counts as unemployment, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness
Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits remain unemployed, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4039.feedback: This pulls together underemployment, discouraged workers, and cyclical unemployment.

PG3-AD-EL-001.q: A student calls the change from AD0 to AD1 an increase in aggregate supply because more output is shown. At a price level of 50, which response fits the diagram?
options: Quantity demanded falls by about 55 units; this is a demand contraction, not a reduction in productive capacity.
Output capacity rises by about 55 units; the horizontal distance measures the shift in long-run supply.
Quantity demanded rises by about 55 units; this is a demand shift, not evidence of increased productive capacity.
Quantity demanded rises by about 155 units; the new quantity is also the size of the demand shift.
PG3-AD-EL-001.feedback: At price 50 the two demand curves show roughly 100 and 155 units. Their difference is about 55. Comparing quantities at a common price identifies an AD shift; it does not measure productive capacity.

PG3-AD-L-001.q: Government purchases rise while private investment partly offsets the increase. The net change is shown by AD0 to AD1. At price level 50, what does the diagram establish about spending and equilibrium output?
options: Desired spending rises by about 35 units; the equilibrium output response still requires aggregate-supply information.
Equilibrium output rises by about 55 units; the common-price distance already includes any price adjustment.
Desired spending rises by about 155 units; the graph identifies that entire amount as the increase in government purchases.
Desired spending rises by about 55 units; the equilibrium output response still requires aggregate-supply information.
PG3-AD-L-001.feedback: AD0 is near 100 and AD1 near 155 at price 50. This is a net common-price demand increase of about 55, after the investment offset. The figure has no supply curve, so it cannot determine the final output increase or separate gross spending changes.

PG3-AD-M-002.q: Which event is most consistent with the shift from AD0 to AD1?
options: Households increase planned consumption at each price level.
Firms cut planned investment at each interest rate.
Input costs rise while planned spending is unchanged.
The price level falls with spending plans otherwise unchanged.
PG3-AD-M-002.feedback: AD1 lies right of AD0: more real output is demanded at each price level. Higher planned consumption can produce that shift; falling investment would shift AD the other way.

PG3-AD-M-004.q: Which event best matches the shift from AD0 to AD1?
options: Foreign income rises, increasing demand for domestic exports.
Production becomes less costly after an input-price decline.
Firms reduce planned investment as their sales outlook weakens.
The domestic price level rises along an unchanged AD curve.
PG3-AD-M-004.feedback: AD1 lies left of AD0. A weaker investment outlook reduces spending at each price level. Export growth would shift demand right, and a change in the price level alone moves along AD.

PG3-AD-L-002.q: Falling confidence reduces consumption while higher government purchases raise spending. The result is the change from AD0 to AD1. What can be inferred about these competing effects?
options: The purchases increase is larger; the graph gives their net effect, not each separate amount.
The consumption reduction is larger; the graph gives their net effect, not each separate amount.
The consumption reduction is larger; its full amount equals the horizontal distance between the curves.
The two effects are equal; the distance between the curves reflects only a lower price level.
PG3-AD-L-002.feedback: AD1 lies left of AD0, so the negative consumption effect dominates. The distance measures the net change at a common price, not either gross effect. A price-level change would be a movement along a curve.

ECON-SP-ELITE-341.q: The economy begins at AD2-AS2. Higher input costs then move supply to AS1 while demand stays fixed. A commentator says the resulting output loss proves demand must also have fallen. Does the graph support that claim?
options: No. Output falls from Y2 to Y1 while the price level rises from P2 to P3; a supply contraction can produce both changes.
No. Output falls from Y1 to Y3 while the price level rises from P1 to P2; a supply contraction can produce both changes.
Yes. The move from Y2/P2 to Y1/P3 requires a demand contraction because supply alone changes only prices.
Yes. The move from Y2/P2 to Y1/P3 shows that lower spending is the cause of every fall in equilibrium output.
ECON-SP-ELITE-341.feedback: On fixed AD2, AS2 to AS1 changes equilibrium from Y2/P2 to Y1/P3. Costlier production lowers output and raises the price level without a demand decline; output alone does not identify the shock.

ECON-SP-ELITE-340.q: Starting at AD1-AS2, higher input costs reduce short-run aggregate supply. Which outcome in the graph illustrates stagflation?
options: Y3/P2: lower output and a higher price level.
Y1/P3: lower output and a higher price level.
Y3/P2: lower output caused by weaker aggregate demand.
Y2/P2: higher output caused by improved productive capacity.
ECON-SP-ELITE-340.feedback: AD1-AS2 is Y1/P1. Moving to AS1 with AD1 fixed gives Y3/P2: output falls and the price level rises. That combination is the adverse-supply pattern, not a demand recession.

ECON-SP-ELITE-312.q: An oil shock moves the economy from AD1-AS2 to AD1-AS1. Policymakers then move demand to AD2. A claim says this response restores the economy to its original condition. What does the diagram show?
options: Output returns to Y1, but prices reach P3 rather than P1; restoring output does not reverse the supply shock.
Output rises to Y2 and prices reach P2; the response overshoots the original output level.
Output returns to Y1 and prices reach P3; this means productive capacity has increased enough to undo the oil shock.
Output remains at Y3 with prices at P2; the stimulus only prevents a further output decline.
ECON-SP-ELITE-312.feedback: The original equilibrium is Y1/P1; the supply shock gives Y3/P2; AD2-AS1 gives Y1/P3. Demand support offsets the output loss at a higher price level and does not restore the original supply conditions.

ECON-SP-ELITE-339.q: Starting at AD1-AS2, the economy ends at AD2-AS1. Which combination of shocks explains the unchanged output level and the change in prices shown?
options: An adverse supply shock and demand stimulus offset in output, while both raise the price level.
A favorable supply shock and demand restraint offset in output, while both lower the price level.
An adverse supply shock and demand restraint reinforce the output loss while their price effects offset.
Demand stimulus alone raises prices while output stays at potential immediately because short-run supply is vertical.
ECON-SP-ELITE-339.feedback: The figure moves from Y1/P1 to Y1/P3. AS shifts left and AD shifts right, with opposing output effects of the depicted sizes. Both shifts raise prices. Unchanged output does not imply that neither curve changed.

ECON-SP-HARD-216.q: At AD2-AS2, demand and productive capacity remain unchanged. How would wage adjustment move the economy toward long-run equilibrium?
options: Wages rise; SRAS contracts, bringing output toward Y1 and prices toward P3.
Wages fall; SRAS expands, bringing output toward Y2 and prices toward P1.
Wages rise; demand contracts, bringing output toward Y1 and prices toward P3.
Wages fall; lower production costs bring output toward Y1 while LRAS shifts left.
ECON-SP-HARD-216.feedback: The starting output Y2 exceeds potential Y1. Upward wage and expected-price pressure shifts SRAS from AS2 toward AS1. On AD2 the long-run endpoint is Y1/P3; capacity and demand need not change.

ECON-SP-HARD-217.q: The economy is at AD1-AS1. If demand and potential output do not change, how would flexible wages help close the gap shown?
options: Lower wages shift SRAS right, raising output from Y3 toward Y1 and lowering prices toward P1.
Higher wages shift SRAS left, lowering output from Y2 toward Y1 and raising prices toward P3.
Lower wages shift LRAS right, raising potential output from Y3 to Y1.
Lower wages shift AD right, moving output from Y3 to Y1 at a higher price level.
ECON-SP-HARD-217.feedback: The graph places current output at Y3, left of potential Y1. Lower wage costs move AS1 toward AS2. The resulting Y1/P1 is reached along AD1, without a capacity change.

ECON-SP-HARD-218.q: A tax increase reduces consumption and aggregate demand. Productive capacity is unchanged, and equilibrium output falls below potential. What kind of gap has opened, and through which curve did the tax increase create it?
options: A recessionary gap caused by a leftward AD shift.
An inflationary gap caused by a rightward AD shift.
A recessionary gap caused by a leftward LRAS shift.
An inflationary gap caused by a movement up an unchanged AD curve.
ECON-SP-HARD-218.feedback: Lower consumption shifts AD left. With potential output unchanged, the resulting output shortfall is a recessionary gap.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9003.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. Starting at AD1-AS2, a lasting demand expansion moves AD to AD2. Wage adjustment then moves SRAS all the way to AS1. Only after this adjustment does a delayed fiscal contraction return AD to AD1. With wages slow to change again, why does this delayed action fail to restore the original equilibrium immediately?
options: It ends at Y3/P2; returning to Y1/P1 now requires wage and cost adjustment toward AS2.
It ends at Y2/P2; returning to Y1/P1 now requires wage and cost adjustment toward AS2.
It ends at Y3/P2; that is the new potential output because the earlier wage adjustment shifted LRAS.
It ends at Y1/P1; restoring the old demand curve is sufficient even though supply has changed.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9003.feedback: The sequence is AD1-AS2 at Y1/P1, AD2-AS2 at Y2/P2, AD2-AS1 at Y1/P3, then AD1-AS1 at Y3/P2. After wages adjusted to the demand expansion, simply restoring old demand creates a new recessionary gap. Subsequent lower wage and expected-price pressures can return SRAS toward AS2.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9004.q: The economy starts at AD1-AS1. Officials choose between allowing wage adjustment to AS2 and expanding demand to AD2. What happens if the full demand expansion takes effect after wage adjustment has already reached AS2?
options: It reaches Y2/P2, above potential; a stimulus sized for the original gap is excessive after self-correction.
It reaches Y3/P3, above potential; a stimulus sized for the original gap is excessive after self-correction.
It reaches Y2/P2, the new potential; combining the policies permanently raises productive capacity.
It reaches Y1/P3; prior wage adjustment has no effect on the endpoint of a fixed demand expansion.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9004.feedback: Either change alone can reach Y1 from the initial gap. Together AD2 and AS2 intersect at Y2/P2, above LRAS. The demand intervention should be reassessed after the supply adjustment.

PM2D1-LRADJ-EB-002.q: An economy produces below potential while aggregate demand remains unchanged. Which wage adjustment would help close the recessionary gap?
options: Rising wages reduce costs and shift SRAS right toward potential output.
Falling wages shift AD left and reduce the output gap.
Rising wages raise potential output by shifting LRAS right.
Falling wages reduce costs and shift SRAS right toward potential output.
PM2D1-LRADJ-EB-002.feedback: A recessionary gap puts downward pressure on wages. Lower labor costs increase short-run aggregate supply, allowing output to rise toward unchanged potential.

PM2D1-LRADJ-L-001.q: Demand has moved the economy to AD2-AS2. With AD2 and productive capacity unchanged, how do the short-run and long-run outcomes compare?
options: Output falls from Y2 to Y1 as wage costs adjust; the price level rises from P2 to P3.
Output rises from Y3 to Y1 as wage costs adjust; the price level falls from P2 to P1.
Output falls from Y2 to Y1 because potential output falls; the price level rises from P2 to P3.
Output stays at Y2 because the demand expansion permanently raises capacity; prices stay at P2.
PM2D1-LRADJ-L-001.feedback: Y2 is above the fixed potential level Y1. Wage and expectation adjustment contracts SRAS toward AS1, leaving output at Y1 and prices at P3. The short-run demand-driven output gain is temporary.

PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-002.q: An economy is below potential, and falling wages begin to increase short-run aggregate supply. Before adjustment is complete, aggregate demand falls further. Without knowing the sizes of these changes, what can be predicted about output?
options: The wage adjustment supports recovery, but the additional demand loss makes the net output change uncertain.
Falling wages guarantee a return to potential before the demand decline can affect output.
The demand decline guarantees falling output even if the supply response is larger.
Both changes reduce potential output because both shift long-run aggregate supply.
PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-002.feedback: Lower wage costs support output, while the new demand decline reduces it. Their relative sizes determine the net movement. Neither change by itself establishes a loss of productive capacity.

PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-004.q: Output is below unchanged potential, but nominal wages are fixed by contracts for one year. Officials predict an immediate recovery caused solely by lower wages. What is wrong with this forecast?
options: The timing is reasonable, but lower wages would contract short-run supply.
The direction is reasonable, but the stated contracts prevent this wage adjustment from occurring immediately.
The forecast fails because returning to potential requires lower productive capacity.
The forecast is valid because fixed wage contracts have no effect on the timing of cost adjustment.
PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-004.feedback: Lower wages could reduce costs and expand short-run supply, but the stipulated contracts prevent that wage channel from operating immediately. The expected direction does not establish the timing.

PG3-AS-L-001.q: A temporary energy bottleneck and a permanent loss of equipment both reduce short-run aggregate supply. Once energy costs normalize, what additional evidence is needed to predict whether wage adjustment can restore the old output level?
options: Whether the price level initially rose; any price rise proves that LRAS stayed fixed.
Whether productive capacity has been restored; lower wage costs alone do not replace the lost equipment.
Whether actual GDP fell; any actual output loss permanently lowers potential output by the same amount.
Whether demand policy can raise spending; a rightward AD shift by itself restores lost productive capacity.
PG3-AS-L-001.feedback: Lower energy costs can reverse a temporary supply restraint. Destroyed equipment may leave productive capacity lower, so restoring the old output level requires evidence that capacity was restored; wage adjustment alone does not replace equipment.

PG3-AS-L-002.q: Lower expected prices and a lasting productivity gain both increase short-run aggregate supply. If expected prices return to their original level while the productivity gain remains, what can be predicted?
options: SRAS must return to its original position because expected prices returned, regardless of productivity.
SRAS cannot move again because a lasting productivity gain prevents expectation effects.
Potential output must fall because higher expected prices erase the physical productivity gain.
Some supply increase can remain, and potential output can be higher; the exact final SRAS position depends on the two contributions.
PG3-AS-L-002.feedback: Returning expected prices reverses only that contribution to SRAS. The productivity gain can still support higher supply and potential output. The final SRAS position depends on the sizes of the original contributions.

PG3-AS-M-002.q: Which event best matches the shift from AS0 to AS1?
options: Lower wage costs make production more profitable at each price level.
Stronger consumer confidence raises planned spending.
An increase in input prices raises production costs.
A lower price level reduces output along the original supply curve.
PG3-AS-M-002.feedback: AS1 lies above and left of AS0, indicating less output supplied at each price level. Higher input costs can produce that contraction; lower costs would move supply the other way.

PG3-AS-M-004.q: Which change could explain the shift from AS0 to AS1 in the diagram?
options: Lower input costs increase short-run aggregate supply.
Higher expected prices reduce short-run aggregate supply.
Higher government purchases increase aggregate demand.
A higher current price level raises output along AS0.
PG3-AS-M-004.feedback: AS1 lies below and right of AS0, so more output is supplied at each price. Lower input costs can explain this shift. Higher expected prices would shift SRAS in the opposite direction.

ECON-SP-ELITE-349.q: What does the path b to d to c show about disinflation when expected inflation adjusts gradually?
options: Unemployment temporarily rises from U2 to U3, then returns to U2 as expectations fall.
Unemployment temporarily rises from U1 to U2, then returns to U1 as expectations fall.
Unemployment rises from U2 to U3 because disinflation permanently raises the natural rate.
Unemployment returns from U3 to U2 through a rise in demand along the unchanged upper SRPC.
ECON-SP-ELITE-349.feedback: The path first moves down SRPC2 from b to d, raising unemployment to U3. Falling expected inflation then shifts the short-run curve down, reaching c at the unchanged natural rate U2.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9047.q: After moving from b to d, inflation is held at the rate shown at d. Supply conditions and natural unemployment stay unchanged. A forecast predicts a return to the natural rate. Which expectation adjustment is consistent with the diagram?
options: Expected inflation falls, shifting the short-run curve through c; staying on SRPC2 would leave the economy at d.
Expected inflation rises, shifting the short-run curve through b; staying on SRPC1 would leave the economy at a.
Expected inflation falls, shifting the short-run curve through c; this permanently lowers natural unemployment from U3 to U2.
Expected inflation is unchanged; demand growth alone moves d to c along SRPC2.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9047.feedback: At the fixed lower inflation rate, c is on SRPC1 at natural unemployment U2, while d remains on SRPC2 at U3. With the supply offset fixed, lower expectations are needed to change the short-run curve.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3010.q: Starting at b, policymakers reduce inflation. Why could the economy reach c directly instead of first passing through d?
options: Expectations and contracts adjust promptly, moving the short-run relationship from SRPC1 to SRPC2 before the demand restraint.
Expectations and contracts adjust promptly, moving the short-run relationship from SRPC2 to SRPC1 before the demand restraint.
Expectations remain fixed, but the lower actual inflation alone moves both unemployment and the short-run curve to c.
Demand restraint permanently lowers natural unemployment, shifting LRPC to c before expectations change.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3010.feedback: The graph places c on the lower SRPC at the same natural unemployment rate as b. Reaching c immediately requires lower expected inflation and prompt contract adjustment; demand restraint with old expectations leads to d.

PM2B3-POL-FB-006.q: A low-capital economy could earn high marginal returns from investment, but unreliable contract enforcement deters investors. Why might improving enforcement alongside investment be more effective than subsidizing machines alone?
options: It addresses investors' ability to retain returns as well as the cost of adding capital.
Machine subsidies already eliminate any risk that investors will lose their returns.
Improved enforcement raises the capital stock immediately without requiring investment.
High marginal returns remove the need for either reliable institutions or investment finance.
PM2B3-POL-FB-006.feedback: High physical returns do not guarantee investment when investors cannot retain the proceeds. Better enforcement addresses that incentive constraint and complements capital accumulation; it does not itself create machines or guarantee catch-up.

PM2B3-POL-H-001.q: With technology and other inputs fixed, successive increases in capital per worker produce smaller additions to output per worker. What does this imply for a policy that relies on capital accumulation alone?
options: It can raise the level of output, but sustaining productivity growth also requires improvements beyond physical capital alone.
It cannot raise output after the first investment because diminishing returns mean a zero marginal product.
It lowers output as soon as marginal gains become smaller than earlier gains.
It preserves the initial output growth rate indefinitely if the same amount of capital is added each year.
PM2B3-POL-H-001.feedback: Capital deepening raises output per worker, but diminishing marginal returns limit repeated gains. Sustained productivity growth requires continuing improvements such as technology or human capital; additional physical capital does not become useless.

PM2B3-POL-LB-001.q: A planner proposes ever larger additions to capital per worker to sustain the initial productivity growth rate indefinitely. Technology and all other productivity determinants remain fixed, and capital has diminishing marginal returns. What weakness in the plan separates a level gain from sustained growth?
options: The plan fails because diminishing returns mean further capital reduces total output per worker.
The plan succeeds because a higher productivity level continues growing even after capital accumulation stops.
The plan succeeds because larger capital stocks prevent marginal returns from diminishing.
The plan assumes capital deepening can sustain its early gains despite diminishing marginal returns and unchanged technology.
PM2B3-POL-LB-001.feedback: Capital additions still raise output, but each unit contributes less. A catch-up increase in the productivity level does not establish a self-sustaining growth mechanism with other productivity determinants fixed.

ECON-SP-HARD-228.q: At a fixed price level, initial desired output is $500 billion. Government purchases rise by $40 billion and MPC is 0.5. Crowding out creates a total $20 billion AD offset, already including induced effects. Under the simple spending multiplier, what is the new quantity of output demanded?
options: $560 billion; subtract the already-total offset from the multiplied spending increase.
$540 billion; subtract the offset from purchases before multiplying both amounts.
$580 billion; the offset does not affect demand after the multiplier operates.
$620 billion; add the offset to the multiplied spending increase.
ECON-SP-HARD-228.feedback: The spending multiplier is 2, so the gross demand increase is $80 billion. Subtract the already-total $20 billion offset once, leaving a $60 billion net increase and $560 billion demanded. Without supply information, this is not a prediction of equilibrium output.

ECON-SP-HARD-229.q: Government purchases and induced spending move demand from AD1 to AD3. If crowding out leaves demand at AD2, how much of the original expansion has been offset?
options: Part of it: final demand remains above AD1 but below AD3.
More than all of it: final demand lies below the original AD1.
None of it: the distance from AD2 to AD3 is additional induced spending.
All of it: reaching AD2 means spending has returned to its initial curve.
ECON-SP-HARD-229.feedback: At a common price AD2 lies between AD1 and AD3. Crowding out reduces the gross expansion but does not reverse it. Identifying the offset requires distinguishing the original, gross and final demand positions.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9024.q: A purchases change first moves AD1 to AD2; induced consumption then moves demand to AD3. Higher interest rates subsequently reduce private spending. Which account fits the directions shown?
options: The direct and induced effects expand demand; the interest-rate effect partly offsets that expansion.
The direct and induced effects contract demand; the interest-rate effect further reduces demand.
The direct and induced effects expand demand; the later private-spending decline is another multiplier expansion.
The first demand change is induced consumption; the second is the original purchases impulse.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9024.feedback: AD2 is right of AD1 and AD3 farther right. The first shift is the direct purchases effect, the next is induced spending, and the reduction in private spending is crowding out. The initial impulse must not be confused with the rounds it induces.

LG-Q-9142.q: A $60 billion tax cut has an MPC of 0.75; an alternative policy raises government purchases by $45 billion. With the same spending multiplier and no crowding out, how do their effects on aggregate demand and their budget costs compare?
options: Both first-round impulses are $60 billion and total shifts $240 billion, because taxes and purchases are identical
The tax cut adds only $45 billion in total, while purchases receive induced spending
Both first-round impulses are $45 billion and total shifts $180 billion, although the budget costs differ
The tax cut first adds $60 billion and ultimately $240 billion, while purchases add only $180 billion
LG-Q-9142.feedback: The tax cut initially raises consumption by 0.75 × $60 billion = $45 billion. Purchases also add $45 billion directly. Multiplying each by 4 gives $180 billion in total, but the tax cut costs the budget $60 billion versus $45 billion for purchases.

PMOE-FX-L-002.q: Foreign demand causes the shift from D0 to D1. With domestic and foreign price levels fixed, how does the exchange-rate response shown affect the original export stimulus?
options: The dollar appreciates 20%, making domestic goods dearer abroad and partly restraining the rise in net exports.
The dollar appreciates 50%, making domestic goods dearer abroad and partly restraining the rise in net exports.
The dollar appreciates 20%, making domestic goods cheaper abroad and reinforcing the rise in net exports.
The dollar appreciates 20%, which establishes that the entire initial increase in export demand is canceled.
PMOE-FX-L-002.feedback: The rate rises from 1.0 to 1.2 foreign-currency units per dollar, a 20% appreciation. At fixed price levels this also is real appreciation, which restrains net exports along the new relationship. It does not measure the size of the original demand shift or prove a full offset.

PMOE-FX-B3-003.q: The dollar market moves from A to B. An importer faces an unchanged foreign-currency price. How do the dollar, traded quantity and dollar cost of the import change?
options: The dollar depreciates 25%, quantity rises 50%, and the import costs about 33.3% more in dollars.
The dollar depreciates 20%, quantity rises 50%, and the import costs 20% more in dollars.
The dollar depreciates 20%, quantity rises 50%, and the import costs 25% more in dollars.
The dollar depreciates 20%, quantity rises about 33.3%, and the import costs 25% less in dollars.
PMOE-FX-B3-003.feedback: The graph gives e: 1.0 to 0.8 and quantity: 100 to 150. Thus e falls 20% and quantity rises 50%. An unchanged foreign price costs 1/0.8 = 1.25 times as many dollars. Reciprocal percentage changes are not symmetric.

PMOE-FX-L-003.q: The dollar market changes from the solid curves to the dashed curve, with price levels fixed. Lower domestic real returns and higher domestic political risk are proposed explanations. What does the figure establish, and what remains unresolved?
options: Dollar supply falls and the dollar appreciates; separate return or risk evidence is needed to distinguish the causes.
Dollar supply rises and the dollar depreciates; the downward rate change rules out a rise in political risk.
Dollar demand rises and the dollar depreciates; depreciation identifies lower domestic returns as the only cause.
Dollar supply rises and the dollar depreciates; separate return or risk evidence is needed to distinguish the causes.
PMOE-FX-L-003.feedback: S1 lies right of S0, and B has a lower exchange rate and greater quantity than A. With fixed prices this is also real depreciation. Both lower returns and greater risk can encourage foreign-asset purchases; the figure does not separately identify them.

PMOE-FX-EL-002.q: A report claims that dollar demand did not change between A and B because the final exchange rate is unchanged. What does the diagram show, and does it reveal which market shift occurred first?
options: Quantity rises from 100 to 150 and D1 differs from D0; the final equilibrium does not identify the order of the shifts.
Quantity rises from 100 to 200 and D1 differs from D0; the unchanged final rate proves demand shifted first.
Quantity rises from 100 to 200, but an unchanged exchange rate means the demand curve remained fixed.
Quantity rises from 100 to 200 and D1 differs from D0; the final equilibrium does not identify the order of the shifts.
PMOE-FX-EL-002.feedback: The figure shows both curves shifting right and quantity doubling from 100 to 200 at rate 1.0. Offsetting effects on the rate do not mean unchanged demand. The final curves reveal no chronology.

PMOE-FX-LB-003.q: Compare demand-first and supply-first adjustment from the solid to the dashed curves. Each market clears before the second shift. Approximately how do the intermediate exchange rates differ, and does the order change the final equilibrium?
options: Demand first gives 1.4 and supply first 0.6; both paths end at B once both shifts occur.
Demand first gives 1.2 and supply first 0.8; both paths end at B once both shifts occur.
Demand first gives 1.2 and supply first 0.8; these different temporary rates imply different final equilibria.
Both intermediate rates are 1.0; an unchanged final rate rules out a temporary exchange-rate response.
PMOE-FX-LB-003.feedback: D1 intersects S0 near 1.2, while D0 intersects S1 near 0.8. The two sequences therefore have different temporary rates but the same final D1-S1 intersection at B. Endpoint evidence cannot establish an unchanged path.

PMOE-FX-M-006.q: What condition defines equilibrium in the market for U.S. dollars?
options: The exchange rate equals the value at which demand for dollars would fall to zero.
Everyone buying dollars has the same reason for doing so as everyone selling dollars.
The quantity of dollars supplied stays fixed regardless of the quantity demanded.
The quantity of dollars demanded equals the quantity supplied at the prevailing exchange rate.
PMOE-FX-M-006.feedback: At the equilibrium exchange rate, the quantity of dollars people want to buy equals the quantity they want to sell. Equality of quantities at that rate, rather than identical motives or curve intercepts, clears the market.

PMOE-FX-LB-001.q: Foreign export demand shifts D0 to D1 and residents' foreign-asset purchases shift S0 to S1. Foreign purchases of domestic assets are unchanged. What can be inferred from the diagram and the separate asset-flow information?
options: The exchange rate rises and gross dollar quantity rises; the asset flows imply higher NCO and therefore higher NX.
The exchange rate is unchanged and gross dollar quantity rises; the increase in gross quantity directly measures the increase in NCO.
The exchange rate is unchanged and gross dollar quantity rises; the unchanged rate implies unchanged NCO despite the asset flows.
The exchange rate is unchanged and gross dollar quantity rises; the asset flows imply higher NCO and therefore higher NX.
PMOE-FX-LB-001.feedback: The final intersection is farther right at the same rate. NCO rises because residents buy more foreign assets with foreign purchases of domestic assets unchanged. In consistent accounts NX equals NCO; gross FX turnover itself is not a measure of that net flow.

PMOE-POL-M-003.q: As NCO-determined supply changes from S0 to S1, how does the dollar change in value?
options: It appreciates 20%, because the foreign-currency price of a dollar rises from 1.0 to 1.2.
It appreciates 50%, because the foreign-currency price of a dollar rises from 1.0 to 1.5.
It depreciates 50%, because a dollar buys 1.5 rather than 1.0 foreign-currency units.
Its value is unchanged; the smaller quantity of dollars supplied affects trading volume alone.
PMOE-POL-M-003.feedback: The graph moves from A at 1.0 to B at 1.5 foreign-currency units per dollar. Each dollar buys more foreign currency, so it appreciates by 50%. The lower NCO-determined quantity is consistent with that rise.

PMOE-POL-B2-001.q: Which fiscal-policy transmission could explain the change from S0 to S1 in this foreign-exchange diagram?
options: A larger deficit raises domestic real rates, reduces NCO and lowers the dollar supply.
A smaller deficit lowers domestic real rates, increases NCO and raises the dollar supply.
A larger deficit raises domestic real rates and increases residents' purchases of foreign assets.
A smaller deficit directly raises foreign demand for domestic exports, shifting dollar supply.
PMOE-POL-B2-001.feedback: S1 is left of S0, indicating lower NCO-determined dollar supply. A larger deficit can reduce national saving, raise real rates and discourage net capital outflow. The currency-market effect comes through asset transactions, not a direct shift in export demand.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9114.q: A monetary contraction reduces investment by $40 billion in an economy already below potential. MPC is 0.75. A timely fiscal program adds a total $100 billion to aggregate demand after induced effects. What is the net demand change, and does the fiscal program fully offset the monetary contraction?
options: AD still falls $60 billion; the fiscal offset softens but does not reverse the contractionary monetary chain
AD rises $60 billion; any positive fiscal offset reverses the money-market contraction
AD rises $240 billion; multiply the already-total fiscal offset by four again
AD falls $160 billion; a fiscal offset cannot affect the same AD curve
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9114.feedback: The investment decline reduces demand by $40/(1 − 0.75) = $160 billion. The already-total fiscal effect offsets $100 billion of that loss, leaving a $60 billion contraction. Applying the multiplier again to the fiscal total would double-count induced spending.

ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4006.q: Demand expands from AD1-AS2 to AD2-AS2. An analyst calls the new output level permanent capacity growth. If demand then stays at AD2, what does the graph imply?
options: Potential remains Y3; rising wage costs move SRAS toward AS1, removing the temporary output gain.
Potential remains Y1; wage adjustment closes the gap by shifting AD2 back to AD1.
Potential remains Y1; rising wage costs move SRAS toward AS1, removing the temporary output gain.
Potential rises to Y2; reaching that output through demand expansion permanently moves LRAS.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4006.feedback: LRAS remains at Y1, while AD2-AS2 is at Y2. Above-potential output raises wage and expected-price pressure, shifting SRAS left toward AS1 and returning output to Y1 on fixed AD2.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9103.q: At AD2-AS2, officials call the increase in output permanent capacity growth. There is no resource or technology change, AD2 stays fixed, and expected prices rise. How do the AD-AS and Phillips-curve models challenge their claim?
options: Output returns to Y3 as SRAS moves toward AS1; rising expected inflation also removes the temporary below-natural unemployment gain.
Output returns to Y1 as SRAS moves toward AS1; this means the natural unemployment rate permanently rises.
Output returns to Y1 as SRAS moves toward AS1; rising expected inflation also removes the temporary below-natural unemployment gain.
Output stays at Y2 as LRAS moves right; rising expected inflation permanently increases productive capacity.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9103.feedback: The graph places LRAS at Y1, not the demand-driven Y2. Higher wage and price expectations move SRAS left with AD2 fixed. In the Phillips model, the upward expectations adjustment returns unemployment to the unchanged natural rate.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9102.q: An adverse supply shock moves the economy from AD1-AS2 to AD1-AS1. While AS1 persists, compare keeping AD1 with expanding demand to AD2. How should the output-restoration claim be evaluated?
options: Expansion reaches Y2/P3 instead of Y1/P2; it overshoots potential and leaves prices above the original P1.
Expansion reaches Y1/P3 instead of Y3/P2; returning to Y1 proves that the original supply conditions have been restored.
Expansion reaches Y1/P1; recovering original output also restores the original price level despite AS1 remaining in place.
Expansion reaches Y1/P3 instead of Y3/P2; it restores output but leaves prices above the original P1.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9102.feedback: At unchanged demand the supply shock gives AD1-AS1, Y3/P2. Accommodation gives AD2-AS1, Y1/P3. It offsets the output loss through greater demand, paying a further price-level increase rather than undoing the supply constraint.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9104.q: At AD1-AS1, wage expectations gradually fall with AD1 fixed. Alternatively, officials could move demand to AD2 before wages adjust. How do the two routes back toward potential compare?
options: Wage adjustment reaches Y2/P1; demand support reaches Y2/P3. Equal output recovery need not give equal prices.
Wage adjustment reaches Y1/P1; demand support reaches Y1/P3. Equal output recovery need not give equal prices.
Wage adjustment reaches Y1/P1; demand support reaches Y1/P3. The latter must therefore have raised productive capacity.
Both routes reach Y1/P1; once output is restored, the price level is independent of how recovery occurred.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9104.feedback: Falling wage/price expectations shift AS1 toward AS2: AD1-AS2 is Y1/P1. Before that adjustment, AD2-AS1 is Y1/P3. Both close the gap under the stated alternatives, with different price levels and timing.

ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4010.q: Demand surprise moves the economy from c to a. Officials promise to maintain the unemployment rate at a with inflation fixed at the rate shown there. With the natural rate unchanged, what happens as expectations catch up?
options: The unemployment target is below U3; maintaining it requires renewed inflation surprises rather than fixed inflation I1.
The unemployment target is U1; holding inflation at I2 permanently lowers the natural rate to that target.
The unemployment target is U1; expected inflation shifts the short-run curve downward until fixed I2 sustains it.
The unemployment target is below U2; maintaining it requires renewed inflation surprises rather than fixed inflation I2.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4010.feedback: Point a is U1/I2, left of natural unemployment U2. Once I2 is expected, b is the corresponding natural-rate equilibrium. Keeping unemployment below natural requires continuing inflation surprises, not the same fixed I2.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9107.q: After the demand surprise c to a, compare repeatedly keeping unemployment at a with accepting b once its inflation rate is expected. What tradeoff does the graph illustrate?
options: Keeping U2 requires renewed inflation surprises; accepting b returns unemployment to U3 while stabilizing inflation at I1.
Keeping U1 requires renewed inflation surprises; accepting b permanently raises the natural rate from U1 to U2.
