Keeping U1 requires renewed inflation surprises; accepting b returns unemployment to U2 while stabilizing inflation at I2.
Both strategies sustain U1 at I2 because the original demand surprise permanently changes the long-run tradeoff.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9107.feedback: a lies left of the LRPC at U2, while b lies on it at I2. Repeatedly pushing unemployment below natural requires inflation above updated expectations. Accepting b gives up the temporary employment gain without changing the natural rate.

ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4012.q: Starting at b, policymakers reduce inflation to I1 before expectations change. If expectations later adapt to I1 and the natural rate stays fixed, how should the transition be interpreted?
options: The path is b-a-c: unemployment first rises, then returns to its natural rate as the short-run curve shifts down.
The path is b-d-c: unemployment first rises, then returns to its natural rate as the short-run curve shifts down.
The path is b-d-c: the return occurs because the natural rate falls permanently from U3 to U2.
The path stops at d: changing expectations cannot alter unemployment when actual inflation stays at I1.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4012.feedback: With initial expectations, I1 intersects SRPC2 at d, U3. Lower expectations shift the curve to SRPC1 and allow c at U2. The change in actual unemployment is temporary; LRPC stays fixed.

ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4013.q: At d after disinflation, actual inflation is held at I1. Compare a credible policy whose lower inflation becomes expected with a policy that leaves expectations at their old level.
options: Lower expectations allow c at U2; old expectations leave d at U3, so commitment alone is not the same as belief.
Lower expectations allow a at U1; old expectations leave d at U3, so commitment alone is not the same as belief.
Lower expectations allow c at U2; this shows credibility permanently reduces the natural rate.
Both cases reach c at U2 immediately, because announcing a fixed actual rate also fixes expectations.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4013.feedback: At I1, the old SRPC2 implies d/U3. Lowering expected inflation shifts the curve down, allowing c/U2 at the same actual inflation. Holding the target is not identical to having the target believed.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9108.q: During the disinflation from b, a credible announcement immediately lowers expectations, but existing wage contracts adjust gradually. Which endpoint and transition-cost claim fit the diagram?
options: a is the eventual endpoint; gradual contract adjustment can still leave temporary unemployment above U2.
c is the eventual endpoint; gradual contract adjustment can still leave temporary unemployment above U2.
c is the eventual endpoint; immediate belief alone eliminates all unemployment costs despite the contract lag.
d is the eventual endpoint; a contract lag permanently prevents the lower expectations from affecting supply.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9108.feedback: At lower inflation I1 and unchanged natural unemployment U2, the endpoint is c. Credibility supports the lower SRPC, but contracts can delay cost adjustment, leaving temporary costs before reaching it.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9115.q: Compare e to d with g to a in the money-market diagram. How do money-supply changes help explain the interest-rate outcomes?
options: e-d combines opposing pressures and lowers the rate from r 3 to r 2; g-a combines reinforcing upward pressures and raises it from r 1 to r 4.
e-d raises the rate from r 2 to r 3 because higher money demand and higher supply both push rates upward.
g-a raises the rate from r 1 to r 4, proving that a money-demand increase has the same rate effect regardless of the supply response.
e-d combines opposing pressures yet raises the rate from r 2 to r 3; g-a combines reinforcing upward pressures and raises it from r 1 to r 4.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9115.feedback: e-d raises both MD and MS: demand pushes rates up while supply pushes them down, with r 3 above r 2 in this drawing. g-a raises MD but reduces MS, reinforcing the increase r 1 to r 4. The net result of opposing shifts depends on their sizes.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9109.q: A report attributes both b-c and c-f to weaker aggregate demand with unchanged expectations. Which correction uses the plotted evidence?
options: b-c fits weaker demand; c-f raises inflation at unchanged unemployment, requiring a change in the short-run relationship.
b-c fits stronger demand; c-f lowers inflation at unchanged unemployment, requiring a change in the short-run relationship.
b-c fits weaker demand; c-f also reflects weaker demand because every change in inflation is movement along one SRPC.
c-f raises inflation at unchanged unemployment; that observation alone proves the change came from expectations rather than supply.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9109.feedback: b-c moves down and right along SRPC1. c and f share U3 but have inflation I2 and I4 on different curves. This second change cannot be a fixed-expectations demand movement; the graph alone need not distinguish expectations from a supply disturbance.

PG4-MM-EL-001.q: A student says a fall in the nominal interest rate from 8% to 6%, with income and the price level unchanged, shifts the money-demand curve right. What is the error?
options: The rate change increases quantity demanded along the existing money-demand curve.
The rate change increases money demand at every interest rate, shifting the entire curve.
The rate change directly increases the fixed money supply while money demand remains constant.
The rate change shifts both money supply and money demand by the same amount.
PG4-MM-EL-001.feedback: The nominal interest rate is the opportunity cost represented on the money-demand curve. A rate change alters quantity demanded along that curve; a change in income or prices would shift it.

PG4-MM-H-001.q: Holding income and the price level fixed, how does a lower nominal interest rate affect the quantity of money people want to hold?
options: It decreases because money earns less interest than before.
It stays unchanged because only the central bank chooses desired money holdings.
It increases because a lower rate directly shifts the central bank's money supply.
It increases because the opportunity cost of holding money falls.
PG4-MM-H-001.feedback: A lower nominal rate reduces the interest forgone by holding money rather than bonds. Quantity demanded therefore rises along the unchanged money-demand curve.

PG4-MM-L-001.q: Suppose the nominal interest rate is temporarily 8% while the displayed money supply stays fixed. What adjustment would move this market toward equilibrium?
options: People want more money than they hold, so bond sales lower bond prices and push the interest rate up.
People hold more money than they want, so bond purchases raise bond prices and push the interest rate down.
People hold more money than they want, so they sell bonds and push the interest rate up.
People want more money than they hold, so the imbalance automatically shifts money supply right.
PG4-MM-L-001.feedback: At 8%, MD0 shows quantity demanded below the fixed supply of 100. People try to exchange excess balances for bonds. Bond prices rise and yields fall toward the plotted equilibrium rate of 6%.

PG4-MM-M-002.q: In a liquidity-preference model where the central bank fixes the nominal quantity of money, why is the money-supply curve vertical?
options: The quantity demanded stays the same at different nominal interest rates.
The interest rate stays fixed regardless of money demand.
The quantity supplied stays the same at different nominal interest rates.
The central bank changes supplied balances whenever the interest rate changes.
PG4-MM-M-002.feedback: The model holds nominal money supply constant at every interest rate. A change in the interest rate can alter quantity demanded, but does not change the supplied quantity under this assumption.

PG4-MM-M-006.q: Which policy action is consistent with the change from MS0 to MS1, holding money demand fixed?
options: An action that increases the money supply, putting downward pressure on the interest rate.
An action that reduces the money supply, putting downward pressure on the interest rate.
An action that reduces the money supply, putting upward pressure on the interest rate.
An action that raises desired money holdings without changing the money supply.
PG4-MM-M-006.feedback: MS1 lies left of MS0, with the rate rising from 4% to 6%. A reduction in money supply produces this response on fixed MD0. A demand shift would be a different change.

PG4-MM-EL-005.q: A student treats higher money demand as higher aggregate spending. Using both panels, what is wrong with that argument for the move from A to B?
options: The rate rises from 2% to 4%; reduced interest-sensitive spending lowers equilibrium output to 105 rather than increasing AD.
The rate rises from 2% to 6%; reduced interest-sensitive spending lowers equilibrium output to 125 rather than increasing AD.
The rate rises from 2% to 4% and output falls to 105 because higher money demand directly lowers productive capacity.
The rate rises from 2% to 4%; wanting more liquid balances is itself extra goods demand, so the output decline must be unrelated.
PG4-MM-EL-005.feedback: The left panel shows MD increasing at fixed money supply, raising the rate from 2% to 4%. The right panel shows AD falling and output moving from 150 to 105. Desired liquid balances and desired goods expenditure are different; the link runs through borrowing costs.

PG4-MM-L-005.q: Which transmission mechanism explains the changes from A to B in both panels?
options: Money supply rises, lowering the rate; stronger interest-sensitive spending expands AD and raises output and prices.
Money demand rises, raising the rate; weaker interest-sensitive spending contracts AD and lowers output and prices.
Money demand rises, raising the rate; lower output reflects a contraction of SRAS rather than lower spending.
Money supply falls, raising the rate; weaker interest-sensitive spending contracts AD and lowers output and prices.
PG4-MM-L-005.feedback: The supply of money stays fixed while MD shifts right. Higher rates reduce spending, shifting AD left along fixed SRAS. The fourth account has a valid transmission direction, but its money-supply trigger is not the one drawn.

PG4-MM-M-010.q: Which mechanism connects A to B in the money market with A to B in the output market?
options: A fall in borrowing costs increases investment and other interest-sensitive spending.
A rise in borrowing costs lowers firms' production costs and expands short-run supply.
A rise in borrowing costs reduces investment and other interest-sensitive spending.
A rise in desired money holdings directly increases spending on goods and services.
PG4-MM-M-010.feedback: The left panel shows a higher rate at B. Higher borrowing costs reduce investment demand; the right panel consequently shows lower AD. A desire to hold money is not itself a demand for goods.

PG4-MM-M-009.q: After the interest-rate change shown on the left, what happens to spending and the output-market equilibrium on the right?
options: Lower interest-sensitive spending shifts AD left; output is 125 and the price level is 50 at B.
Lower interest-sensitive spending shifts AD left; output is 105 and the price level is 45 at B.
Lower production costs shift SRAS right; output is 105 and the price level is 45 at B.
Only a movement along AD occurs; output is 105 and the price level is 45 with spending plans unchanged.
PG4-MM-M-009.feedback: B is at output 105 and price 45. Higher interest rates reduce planned spending at a given price level, shifting AD rather than moving along it. SRAS is unchanged.

PG4-MPT-M-003.q: Which output-market response matches the monetary change shown across the panels?
options: Borrowing costs restrain spending; AD shifts left to an equilibrium at output 105 and price level 40.
Borrowing costs restrain spending; AD shifts left to an equilibrium at output 100 and price level 45.
Borrowing costs lower production costs; SRAS shifts right to output 100 and price level 45.
Output 100 and price level 45 result from moving along unchanged AD when money supply falls.
PG4-MPT-M-003.feedback: The rate rises as money supply contracts. Interest-sensitive spending falls, shifting AD left; the right-panel B is output 100, price 45, on unchanged SRAS.

PM2C3-LPMM-L-001.q: The money market moves from e to d as money demand and supply both increase. What can be inferred about their competing effects on the interest rate?
options: The demand increase more than offsets the rate-reducing supply effect, so the rate rises.
The supply increase more than offsets the rate-raising demand effect, so the rate falls.
The effects offset exactly, so the rate stays at its original level.
The rate rises because increasing the money supply reinforces the upward pressure from demand.
PM2C3-LPMM-L-001.feedback: e is at r 2 and d at the higher r 3. Increased demand pushes the rate up and increased supply pushes it down. The rise shown identifies a larger demand effect; it does not change the usual separate effects.

PM2C3-LPMM-LB-002.q: A commentator says the move from e to d proves that expanding money supply raises interest rates. How does the diagram bear on this claim?
options: The rate falls from r 3 to r 2, with the supply expansion's downward pressure exceeding the demand increase.
The rate rises from r 2 to r 3, confirming that supply expansion by itself pushes rates upward.
The rate stays at r 2 because simultaneous increases in supply and demand must offset exactly.
The rate rises from r 2 to r 3, but money demand also rises; its upward pressure exceeds the supply expansion's downward pressure.
PM2C3-LPMM-LB-002.feedback: The observed increase is from r 2 to r 3 with both curves shifting right. Holding demand fixed, more money supply lowers the rate. The joint outcome therefore cannot be attributed to that supply effect alone.

PM2C3-LPMM-L-006.q: Starting at e, money demand changes to MD2 and the central bank chooses MS2. Has that choice kept the interest rate at its original value? What adjustment would be needed if not?
options: No; d is below the original rate, so holding that rate requires less money than MS2 supplies.
Yes; increasing money supply always offsets any increase in money demand exactly.
No; d is above the original rate, so the central bank must reduce supply further to lower it.
No; d is above the original rate, so holding that rate requires more money than MS2 supplies.
PM2C3-LPMM-L-006.feedback: The original rate is r 2 at e; d has r 3, above r 2. On MD2, the quantity demanded at r 2 exceeds Qm2, so a larger money supply would be required. The direction follows from the actual under-offset shown.

PM2C3-LPMM-LB-001.q: At the interest rate marked by b, money supply is MS2 and demand is MD2. Compare the initial portfolio adjustment with a central-bank sale that reduces supply to MS1 before the rate changes.
options: Excess balances prompt bond purchases and downward rate pressure; the sale instead makes e the new equilibrium.
Excess balances prompt bond sales and upward rate pressure; the sale makes a the new equilibrium.
A shortage of balances prompts bond sales; reducing supply leaves d as the equilibrium.
Excess balances prompt bond purchases and downward rate pressure; the sale instead makes a the new equilibrium.
PM2C3-LPMM-LB-001.feedback: At b's r 4, desired balances on MD2 are Qm1 while supply is Qm2. Attempts to buy bonds with excess money push rates downward. Reducing supply to MS1 before that adjustment makes MD2 intersect it at a, not e on MD1.

PG5-PC-H-010.q: With expected inflation and supply conditions fixed, what short-run tradeoff does a downward-sloping Phillips curve describe?
options: Lower unemployment is associated with lower inflation.
Lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation.
Unemployment stays fixed at its natural rate at every inflation rate.
A change in actual inflation necessarily changes expected inflation by the same amount.
PG5-PC-H-010.feedback: Along a given short-run Phillips curve, demand conditions that lower unemployment are associated with higher inflation. A change in expected inflation or supply conditions can instead shift the curve.

PG5-PC-L-012.q: Later observations put unemployment at the rate shown at A, but inflation stays above A's level. Which evidence would support a higher short-run Phillips curve crossing the same LRPC, rather than a vertical short-run curve?
options: Unemployment remains 2.5%, and wage-setting expectations rise with sustained inflation while labor-market structure and supply conditions stay unchanged.
Unemployment remains 5%, and a higher price level alone proves the short-run curve has become vertical.
Unemployment remains 5%, and unchanged expectations explain a lasting upward SRPC shift with no other supply change.
Unemployment remains 5%, and wage-setting expectations rise with sustained inflation while labor-market structure and supply conditions stay unchanged.
PG5-PC-L-012.feedback: A is at unemployment 5% and inflation 2.5%. Higher expected inflation can raise SRPC while the same natural rate preserves LRPC. An observed price level or unchanged unemployment alone does not establish that expectations have adjusted.

PG5-PC-M-009.q: What does this LRPC imply about a policy that permanently maintains higher inflation?
options: Long-run unemployment remains 5%; higher sustained inflation does not buy a permanent unemployment reduction.
Long-run unemployment remains 2.5%; higher sustained inflation does not buy a permanent unemployment reduction.
Long-run unemployment starts at 5% but falls permanently as policy moves upward along LRPC.
Unemployment remains 5% at every short-run point because LRPC also fixes the slope of SRPC.
PG5-PC-M-009.feedback: LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5%. Once expectations adjust, a higher sustained inflation rate changes the inflation coordinate rather than the natural unemployment rate. Short-run deviations can still occur.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3004.q: Compare a demand boom that temporarily lowers unemployment with a reform that reduces structural unemployment. Which can change the natural unemployment rate?
options: The demand boom permanently lowers the natural rate; the reform affects only inflation.
Neither can change the natural rate because it is determined by the price level.
The structural reform can lower the natural rate; the demand boom alone changes actual unemployment around that benchmark.
Both must raise the natural rate because lower unemployment requires higher inflation.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3004.feedback: Demand surprises can move actual unemployment temporarily below natural unemployment. A persistent reduction in structural unemployment can lower the natural rate itself and shift the long-run Phillips curve left.

PG3-MEQ-L-003.q: A student attributes the move from A to B to increased aggregate supply. What do the direction of the changes and the fixed curve imply?
options: Supply increased: output rises and the price level falls along unchanged AD0.
Demand increased: output and the price level rise along unchanged AS0.
Supply increased: output and the price level rise because the movement is along unchanged AS0.
Demand decreased: the higher price level at B is the result of reduced spending.
PG3-MEQ-L-003.feedback: B is above and right of A, where AD1 intersects unchanged AS0. More demand raises both output and prices in this short-run diagram. Moving along AS0 does not mean that aggregate supply shifted.

PG3-MEQ-L-004.q: Refer to the ADAS graph with points A, B, C and D. The economy begins at A. A supply disruption moves AS0 to AS1, giving D, and remains in place. Compare two fiscal targets while AS1 stays fixed: restore the original output, or restore the original price level. Which comparison follows from the drawn straight AS1 line, extended if needed?
options: Restoring output reaches C at 75/150; restoring the original price gives output 50 and requires further demand contraction.
Restoring output reaches C at 75/150; this also restores the original purchasing-power conditions because output is unchanged.
Both targets reach A at 75/100 because fiscal expansion shifts the disrupted supply curve back.
Restoring output reaches C at 75/150; restoring the original price gives output 25 and requires further demand contraction.
PG3-MEQ-L-004.feedback: A is (75,100) and D is (50,125). With AS1 fixed, output 75 requires C at price 150. AS1 passes through D (50,125) and C (75,150), so its equation is P = Y + 75; at P = 100, Y = 25. Moving from D to that lower-price point requires lower AD and further output loss. Fiscal demand policy does not remove the supply disruption.

PG3-MEQ-L-001.q: A student claims that the demand increase from AD0 to AD1 permanently raises output above potential. Which account of the short-run and long-run equilibria challenges that claim?
options: The economy first reaches A, then approaches C as wage costs fall; output returns to unchanged potential.
The economy first reaches D, then approaches B as wage costs rise; output returns to unchanged potential.
The economy first reaches D, then approaches B because rising wages permanently reduce potential output.
D remains the long-run equilibrium because demand growth shifts LRAS to its output level.
PG3-MEQ-L-001.feedback: The short-run AD1-SRAS0 intersection is D, right of LRAS at 100. Wage adjustment moves supply toward SRAS1 and equilibrium toward B on LRAS. The demand-driven output gain is temporary even though prices remain higher.

PG3-MEQ-H-002.q: Which event best matches the joint shift from SRAS0/LRAS0 to SRAS1/LRAS1?
options: Destruction of productive capital raises production costs and lowers potential output.
A productivity improvement lowers production costs and raises potential output.
Lower expected prices increase short-run supply without changing productive capacity.
Higher consumer confidence raises spending without changing production costs.
PG3-MEQ-H-002.feedback: Both supply curves move right, with LRAS moving from 100 to 115 and SRAS moving down/right. A productivity gain can explain both lower costs and greater capacity. Lower expectations alone would not move LRAS.

LG-Q-336.q: In the value-of-money graph, the economy moves from a to b. Velocity may change. A nominal wage rises in the same proportion as the implied price level, with technology and labor supplies unchanged. What is consistent with monetary neutrality?
options: Prices and the nominal wage rise by one-third; the real wage is unchanged.
Prices and the nominal wage double; the real wage is unchanged.
Prices and the nominal wage rise by one-third; the real wage also rises by one-third.
Prices fall by one-quarter, so an unchanged real wage requires a one-quarter nominal-wage increase.
LG-Q-336.feedback: The graph gives value of money 2 at a and 1.5 at b. Their reciprocal price levels are 1/2 and 2/3, a one-third increase. Proportional nominal wage growth leaves the real wage unchanged; nominal changes alone do not raise real productive capacity. With real output fixed, this graph requires velocity to fall to two-thirds of its initial value; it is not the fixed-velocity quantity-theory case.

PG4-MPT-H-001.q: Which explanation fits A to B across the two panels?
options: Less money supply raises the rate, restrains interest-sensitive spending and lowers output and prices through AD.
More money supply lowers the rate, stimulates interest-sensitive spending and raises output and prices through AD.
More money demand raises the rate, restrains spending and lowers output and prices through AD.
More money supply lowers the rate and raises output by shifting SRAS right rather than changing spending.
PG4-MPT-H-001.feedback: The left panel shows MS increasing and the rate falling from 6% to 4%. The right panel shows higher AD, output and prices on unchanged SRAS. This is spending transmission, not a supply-capacity change.

PG4-MPT-H-002.q: What explains the changes from A to B in the two panels?
options: Money demand increases; higher borrowing costs restrain spending, shifting AD left on unchanged SRAS.
Money supply expands; lower borrowing costs stimulate spending, shifting AD right on unchanged SRAS.
Money supply contracts; lower productive capacity directly shifts SRAS left while AD stays fixed.
Money supply contracts; higher borrowing costs restrain spending, shifting AD left on unchanged SRAS.
PG4-MPT-H-002.feedback: MS1 lies left of MS0, raising the rate from 2.75% to 4% on unchanged MD0. Spending and AD fall, producing lower output and prices along the same SRAS. Higher money demand could give similar rate pressure, but is not the change shown.

ECON-SP-ELITE-318.q: Which explanation connects the changes from MS1 to MS2 and AD1 to AD2?
options: Money supply falls, raising the rate and reducing investment and aggregate demand.
Money supply rises, lowering the rate and increasing investment and aggregate demand.
Money demand rises, raising the rate and reducing investment and aggregate demand.
Money supply falls, raising the rate and lowering output by reducing long-run productive capacity.
ECON-SP-ELITE-318.feedback: MS2 is left of MS1, with the rate rising from r 1 to r 2. Lower investment then reduces demand from AD1 to AD2. The money-demand curve and productive capacity are not the mechanisms that changed.

PG4-MPT-M-001.q: How does interest-sensitive spending connect the two panels' move from A to B?
options: Spending rises as borrowing costs fall; output reaches 150 and the price level 60 on the new AD curve.
Spending rises as borrowing costs fall; output 125 and price 56.25 are reached by a movement along unchanged AD.
Output 125 and price 56.25 result from lower production costs shifting SRAS, with planned spending unchanged.
Spending rises as borrowing costs fall; output reaches 125 and the price level 56.25 on the new AD curve.
PG4-MPT-M-001.feedback: The rate falls from 6% to 4%, encouraging spending. The right-panel B is at output 125 and price 56.25 where higher AD intersects unchanged SRAS. A borrowing-cost change shifts spending plans rather than merely changing the price level along AD.

PG4-MPT-EL-002.q: A student says the central bank directly chose the real-output level at B. Which explanation uses the mechanism and evidence in both panels?
options: Money supply falls from 125 to 100, raising the rate from 2.75% to 4%; lower spending then reduces output.
Money supply falls from 150 to 100, raising the rate from 4% to 6%; lower spending then reduces output.
Money supply falls from 125 to 100; matching money and output quantities means the bank directly sets real GDP.
Money supply falls from 125 to 100, and output falls because the policy directly reduces productive capacity.
PG4-MPT-EL-002.feedback: The monetary instrument changes money supply, not an output quota. The left panel supplies the rate response; borrowing costs affect investment and AD, with the output result determined by the right-panel intersection.

PG4-MPT-L-002.q: What economic response connects the move from A to B in the two panels?
options: Money supply rises and the rate falls; stronger spending raises output and the price level on unchanged SRAS.
Money supply falls and the rate rises; weaker spending lowers output and the price level on unchanged SRAS.
Money demand rises and the rate rises; weaker spending lowers output and the price level on unchanged SRAS.
Money supply falls and the rate rises; output falls because policy shifts LRAS left.
PG4-MPT-L-002.feedback: The graph shows a leftward money-supply shift at fixed money demand, followed by lower AD. Higher rates restrain spending; output and prices fall along unchanged SRAS. This does not establish a loss of productive capacity.

ECON-SP-HARD-227.q: Read the policy path in reverse, from MS2 to MS1. Which mechanism explains the associated aggregate-demand change?
options: The money supply expands, the rate falls, and investment raises AD from AD2 toward AD1.
The money supply contracts, the rate rises, and investment lowers AD from AD2 toward AD1.
The money supply expands and the rate falls, but the resulting AD change is a movement along a fixed demand curve.
Money demand falls rather than money supply changing, so investment raises AD from AD2 toward AD1.
ECON-SP-HARD-227.feedback: MS1 is right of MS2, with a lower interest rate r 1. The expansion stimulates investment and shifts AD from the leftward AD2 toward AD1. The graph distinguishes the policy supply change from a demand change in the money market.

LG-Q-158.q: Which variables belong in the money-market model used to explain monetary-policy transmission?
options: Money supply, money demand and the nominal interest rate.
Aggregate demand, short-run supply and real output.
Government purchases, tax revenue and the budget deficit.
Capital per worker, productivity and technological progress.
LG-Q-158.feedback: The money market relates desired money holdings to the supplied quantity at different nominal interest rates. Its equilibrium rate affects interest-sensitive spending in the aggregate-demand model.

LG-Q-9053.q: A monetary contraction raises interest rates and reduces aggregate demand by $240 billion. MPC is 0.75, and investment is the only autonomous spending component that changes. What investment change accounts for the total demand loss?
options: Investment fell $960 billion after rates rose; divide the total loss by MPC
Investment fell $60 billion after rates rose; the multiplier converts that impulse to the total AD loss
Investment fell $240 billion before rates changed; the AD loss is the autonomous impulse
Investment rose $60 billion after rates fell; the money shift is expansionary
LG-Q-9053.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1 − 0.75) = 4. Dividing the $240 billion total demand loss by 4 gives a $60 billion autonomous investment decline, occurring after the rate increase and before induced spending falls.

LG-Q-9055.q: A monetary expansion lowers rates and raises investment by $40 billion. A separate loss of confidence reduces investment by $25 billion. With MPC = 0.5, what is the net change in aggregate demand?
options: Right $80 billion: ignore the confidence loss because rates fell
Left $30 billion: reverse the effect of a net investment increase
Right $15 billion: include both impulses but omit induced spending
Right $30 billion: multiply the net $15 billion autonomous investment rise
LG-Q-9055.feedback: The autonomous investment effects net to $15 billion. The spending multiplier is 2, so total demand rises $30 billion. The monetary stimulus must be combined with the confidence effect before the multiplier is applied.

LG-Q-9056.q: The interest rate rises by the same amount in two economies. Investment falls by $20 billion in A and $5 billion in B. Both have MPC = 0.8 and no other shocks. What explains the difference in their total demand responses?
options: AD falls $25 billion in A and $100 billion in B; weaker investment sensitivity magnifies the effect
AD falls $100 billion in both; identical rate changes guarantee identical spending changes
AD falls $100 billion in A and $25 billion in B; B has weaker investment sensitivity to the rate change
AD falls $20 billion in A and $5 billion in B; the multiplier is irrelevant to rate-induced spending
LG-Q-9056.feedback: Both multipliers equal 5, giving demand declines of $100 billion and $25 billion. With the same rate increase and multiplier, the difference reflects investment sensitivity, not reserve accounting.

LG-Q-9059.q: A monetary contraction reduces investment by $40 billion, with MPC = 0.8. A fiscal program adds $200 billion to aggregate demand in total after induced effects. Compare implementing it immediately with implementing it only after the original contraction has ended.
options: Both timings offset exactly because equal dollar effects guarantee equal stabilization
Immediate AD rises $800 billion because the total fiscal effect must be multiplied again
Immediate AD falls $200 billion because fiscal and monetary shifts cannot offset
Immediate effects offset; the delayed program can create excess demand after the original gap closes
LG-Q-9059.feedback: The monetary effect is −40/(1 − 0.8) = −$200 billion, so the immediate fiscal total offsets it. If the program arrives after the original gap closes, the same stimulus can create excess demand. A total effect should not be multiplied again.

LG-Q-9064.q: Policymakers want to reduce aggregate demand by $300 billion. MPC is 0.5, and each one-percentage-point increase in the interest rate reduces investment by $50 billion. Under this spending model, how much must the rate rise?
options: 3 percentage points
6 percentage points
1.5 percentage points
2 percentage points
LG-Q-9064.feedback: The multiplier is 2. A $300 billion total demand reduction requires investment to fall $150 billion. At $50 billion per percentage point, that requires a 3-percentage-point rate increase.

LG-Q-9072.q: A reduction in money supply raises the interest rate when money demand is fixed. Now suppose money demand also falls. Without the relative sizes of the shifts, what can be predicted about the interest-rate and spending responses?
options: Supply contraction alone raises rates; the combined transmission direction remains uncertain.
Supply contraction dominates; rates rise, investment falls and aggregate demand falls.
Demand contraction dominates; rates fall, investment rises and aggregate demand rises.
The contractions cancel; rates, investment and aggregate demand all remain unchanged.
LG-Q-9072.feedback: A supply reduction puts upward pressure on the rate, while lower money demand puts downward pressure on it. Without their relative sizes, the net rate movement and the resulting investment and AD directions remain uncertain.

LG-Q-9131.q: In a fixed-price spending model, monetary tightening reduces investment by $90 billion while improved business expectations independently raise autonomous investment by $30 billion. MPC is 0.6, with no taxes, imports or further interest-rate feedbacks. What is the net AD change, and what independent investment recovery would exactly offset the monetary effect?
options: AD shifts left $150 billion; a $90 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts left $225 billion; a $30 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts left $60 billion; a $150 billion recovery would cancel it.
AD shifts right $150 billion; a $90 billion recovery would cancel it.
LG-Q-9131.feedback: Net autonomous investment changes by −90 + 30 = −$60 billion. The multiplier is 2.5, so AD falls $150 billion. An independent $90 billion recovery would cancel the autonomous monetary loss before any multiplication.

LG-Q-9132.q: The Fed wants to reduce aggregate demand by $300 billion. MPC is 0.75, and each one-percentage-point rise in the interest rate lowers investment by $25 billion. Under these assumptions, how much must the rate rise?
options: 3 percentage points
4 percentage points
12 percentage points
1 percentage point
LG-Q-9132.feedback: A multiplier of 4 means investment must fall $75 billion to lower total demand by $300 billion. Dividing by $25 billion per percentage point gives a 3-percentage-point rate increase.

LG-Q-9138.q: Compare the displayed money-supply change with a counterfactual in which interest rates respond but firms no longer change investment. Which link would fail, and what does the original money-market panel establish?
options: The rate-to-investment link fails; the original rate stays at r 1, consistent with a flat-rate liquidity-trap segment.
The rate-to-investment link fails; the original rate changes from r 1 to r 2, so that panel does not show a liquidity trap.
The supply-to-rate link fails; the original rate changes from r 1 to r 2 despite the assumed investment insensitivity.
The rate-to-investment link fails; the original rate change proves policy has the same output effect even when investment stops responding.
LG-Q-9138.feedback: The figure shows the rate moving from r 1 to r 2 as supply contracts. The hypothetical failure is farther along the chain: the rate no longer changes investment. A rate-responsive money market is different from the flat near-zero-rate case used to illustrate a liquidity trap.

PG5-PC-M-002.q: At the natural unemployment rate shown, how much higher is inflation on SRPC1 than on SRPC0, and what could explain the difference with supply conditions unchanged?
options: 3 percentage points; higher expected inflation shifts the short-run curve upward.
3.6 percentage points; higher expected inflation shifts the short-run curve upward.
3.6 percentage points; a fall in the natural unemployment rate moves LRPC left.
3.6 percentage points; a change in actual inflation alone moves the economy along SRPC0.
PG5-PC-M-002.feedback: At unemployment 5%, SRPC0 gives inflation 3% and SRPC1 gives 6.6%, a 3.6-point gap. With supply conditions unchanged, higher expectations can explain the curve shift. The LRPC stays fixed.

PG5-PC-X-005.q: What does the diagram imply about the natural unemployment rate when SRPC changes from SRPC0 to SRPC1?
options: It remains 5%; shifting the short-run inflation relationship does not itself change the long-run unemployment benchmark.
It remains 6%; shifting the short-run inflation relationship does not itself change the long-run unemployment benchmark.
It becomes 6% because point B always determines the natural rate, even off LRPC.
It remains 5%, so unemployment cannot deviate from 5% anywhere on either short-run curve.
PG5-PC-X-005.feedback: LRPC stays vertical at 5%. Point B is a short-run observation at 6% unemployment, not a new natural-rate marker. Short-run and long-run unemployment need not coincide.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.q: After a demand surprise moves the economy from c to a, actual inflation is held at the rate shown at a. Compare fully adjusted expectations with expectations remaining at their old level.
options: Full adjustment brings the economy to c at U2; old expectations keep it at d at U3.
Full adjustment brings the economy to b at U2 because expectations permanently raise the natural rate.
Both cases reach b immediately because holding actual inflation constant also fixes expected inflation.
Full adjustment brings the economy to b at U2; old expectations keep it at a at U1.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.feedback: At I2, a lies on SRPC1 below natural unemployment and b lies on SRPC2 at U2. Adapting expectations moves the short-run relationship; maintaining actual inflation alone is not the same adjustment.

ECON-SP-ELITE-326.q: How should the change from c to f be interpreted in the short-run Phillips diagram?
options: Inflation rises at unchanged unemployment, indicating a shift of the short-run relationship.
Inflation falls at unchanged unemployment, indicating a shift of the short-run relationship.
Inflation rises at unchanged unemployment, indicating a demand-driven movement along SRPC1.
Unemployment rises at unchanged inflation, indicating a movement along SRPC1.
ECON-SP-ELITE-326.feedback: c and f share unemployment U3 but have inflation I2 and I4 on different curves. The change therefore involves an upward SRPC shift, not a movement along one fixed curve.

ECON-SP-MEDIUM-162.q: Supply conditions and the natural rate are unchanged, so only expected inflation can shift the short-run Phillips curve. What explains the change from c to f?
options: Higher expected inflation raises inflation at the same unemployment rate.
Lower expected inflation reduces inflation at the same unemployment rate.
Higher actual inflation moves the economy along the original SRPC without changing expectations.
Lower natural unemployment shifts the long-run benchmark to U3.
ECON-SP-MEDIUM-162.feedback: f lies above c at the same unemployment rate U3, on the higher short-run curve. With other shifters excluded, this identifies higher expected inflation.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9048.q: What can be inferred when the economy's short-run relationship changes from SRPC1 to SRPC2?
options: Inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate; expectations or a supply disturbance could explain the shift.
Inflation is lower at a given unemployment rate; expectations or a supply disturbance could explain the shift.
Inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate; the graph alone proves that expected inflation rose.
Inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate because stronger demand moved the economy along unchanged SRPC1.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9048.feedback: SRPC2 lies above SRPC1. The less favorable short-run tradeoff can result from higher expectations or an adverse supply disturbance; the shift itself does not identify which cause occurred.

PM2B3-PROD-EB-002.q: Capital per worker doubles from 20 to 40, while output per worker rises from about 28.53 to 36.37. Employment is unchanged. A report says total output must also have doubled. Which correction is appropriate?
options: Output rises 100%; doubling capital always doubles output
Output rises about 7.84%; subtracting productivity levels directly gives a percentage
Output falls about 21.6%; use the higher productivity as the initial value
Output rises about 27.5%, not 100%; fixed employment makes total output grow by that same percentage
PM2B3-PROD-EB-002.feedback: Total output equals output per worker times employment. With employment fixed, its growth is (36.37/28.53 − 1) × 100, about 27.5%, not 100%. A doubling of one input need not double output.

PM2B3-PROD-FB-004.q: Use the displayed coordinates for A and B. Approximately how much does output per worker rise, and what would another equal addition to capital imply with other inputs fixed?
options: About 21.6%; the next equal capital addition would produce a smaller output gain.
About 27.5%; the next equal capital addition would produce a smaller output gain.
About 27.5%; the next equal capital addition would produce an equal output gain.
About 7.84%; the next capital addition would reduce the total level of output per worker.
PM2B3-PROD-FB-004.feedback: Output per worker rises from 28.53 to 36.37, so growth is 7.84/28.53 ≈ 27.5%. The curve flattens at higher capital levels: further equal additions give smaller positive gains, not equal gains or falling total output.

PM2B3-PROD-H-001.q: With technology and other inputs fixed, capital per worker increases along a rising production function with diminishing marginal returns. What would another equal addition to capital per worker imply?
options: A smaller additional output gain because the marginal product of capital declines.
A larger additional output gain because the marginal product of capital rises.
A smaller additional output gain because technology has deteriorated as the economy moves along the curve.
A fall in the level of output per worker because declining marginal returns mean negative marginal returns.
PM2B3-PROD-H-001.feedback: Diminishing marginal returns mean that equal additional amounts of capital yield progressively smaller positive output gains. They do not imply deteriorating technology or negative total output growth.

PM2B3-SRC-EB-002.q: Two economies start at A and B on this productivity curve. Each adds the same small amount of capital per worker, with other inputs fixed. Which comparison follows?
options: The gain is larger near A; capital has a higher marginal product there.
The gain is larger near B; capital has a higher marginal product there.
The gain is larger near A because total output per worker is already higher there.
The gain is zero near B because a smaller marginal product means capital adds nothing.
PM2B3-SRC-EB-002.feedback: The curve is steeper near A than B, indicating a larger marginal output gain at A. B has higher total productivity, but that does not imply a higher marginal gain from capital.

PM2B3-PROD-L-001.q: Two otherwise similar economies begin at A and B. Each receives the same small addition to capital per worker. What does the figure establish about catch-up?
options: The marginal gain is larger at A, but that advantage alone does not guarantee convergence.
The marginal gain is larger at B, but that advantage alone does not guarantee convergence.
The marginal gain is larger at A, which guarantees it will overtake B regardless of institutions or technology.
The productivity level is higher at B, so A cannot gain output from any additional capital.
PM2B3-PROD-L-001.feedback: A lies on the steeper part of the curve, so its marginal gain is larger. Catch-up still depends on accumulation and complementary conditions; the curve does not guarantee that the poorer economy overtakes the richer one.

PM2B3-PROD-LB-002.q: Output per worker changes from A to B, while employment falls by 25%. A report concludes that higher productivity must mean higher total output. Is that conclusion supported?
options: No. Productivity rises about 27.5%, but total output falls about 4.4% after the employment decline.
Yes. Productivity rises about 40%, so total output rises about 5% after the employment decline.
Yes. Productivity rises about 27.5%; subtracting 25% gives a total-output increase of about 2.5%.
No. Productivity itself falls about 4.4%, because employment is part of the vertical-axis measure.
PM2B3-PROD-LB-002.feedback: The plotted productivity ratio is 36.37/28.53 ≈ 1.2748. Total output changes by 1.2748 × 0.75 − 1 ≈ −4.4%. A productivity gain and an employment decline can therefore coexist with lower total output.

43220.q: In the loanable-funds model, why does firms' desired investment form the demand for funds?
options: Investment projects create demand for finance, and higher real borrowing costs make fewer projects worthwhile.
Households supply funds for firms, so investment is the saving-supply schedule.
The central bank fixes investment at each rate, so desired borrowing is independent of financing costs.
Higher real borrowing costs make every investment project more profitable, increasing desired borrowing.
43220.feedback: Firms seek finance for investment projects. A higher real interest rate raises financing costs, making fewer projects worthwhile and reducing desired borrowing along the investment-demand schedule.

43225.q: Which variable acts as the price coordinating saving and investment in the loanable-funds market?
options: The quantity of loanable funds.
The real interest rate.
The government budget balance.
The stock of productive capital.
43225.feedback: The real interest rate is the return to supplying funds and the real cost of borrowing. Changes in that price affect saving supplied and investment demanded.

43224.q: The real interest rate rises from 8% to 10% along unchanged saving-supply and investment-demand curves. How do the quantities supplied and demanded respond?
options: Saving supplied rises and investment demanded falls.
Saving supplied falls and investment demanded rises.
Both quantities rise because the same interest rate applies to savers and borrowers.
Both schedules shift right because the real interest rate changes.
43224.feedback: A higher real rate encourages saving and makes fewer investment projects worthwhile. These are movements along the fixed schedules, not shifts of the schedules themselves.

43249.q: Which event could explain the movement from A to B with the other determinants unchanged?
options: A deterioration in the government budget lowers national saving at each real interest rate.
An improvement in the government budget raises national saving at each real interest rate.
An investment tax credit raises desired investment at each real interest rate.
Reduced expected project profitability lowers desired investment at each real interest rate.
43249.feedback: The graph shows saving supply moving right from S0 to S1 while D0 stays fixed. A budget improvement can increase public and national saving. Investment incentives instead change demand for funds.

43252.q: Government purchases fall while output is fixed and the consumption schedule is unchanged at each real rate. Which account connects this policy to the move from A to B?
options: Higher national saving lowers the rate from 8% to 6%, raising investment from 80 to 120 along D0.
Higher national saving lowers the rate from 8% to 4%, raising investment from 80 to 160 along D0.
Higher national saving lowers the rate from 8% to 6%; investment rises to 120 because D0 shifts right.
The fall from 8% to 6% first raises government saving, so the observed supply shift is a response to the rate.
43252.feedback: With Y and consumption at each rate fixed, lower G raises national saving. The supply increase moves equilibrium from 80/8 to 120/6. The resulting investment response is along unchanged D0, not an independent demand shift.

43255.q: A report calls the increase in investment from A to B a rightward shift of investment demand. How should the displayed change be classified?
options: Investment rises by 80 units along D0 because the saving-supply shift lowers the rate.
Investment rises by 40 units because a lower rate shifts D0 right at every real rate.
Investment rises by 40 units because stronger project profitability shifts D0 while S0 stays fixed.
Investment rises by 40 units along D0 because the saving-supply shift lowers the rate.
43255.feedback: The equilibrium quantity rises from 80 to 120 on unchanged D0, a 40-unit increase. The initiating shift is in saving supply; lower financing costs induce movement along investment demand.

43261.q: An analyst measures the saving-supply shift using only the change in equilibrium quantity from A to B. Is that measure correct for this graph?
options: No. Supply shifts left 60 units at a common rate, while equilibrium investment falls only 20 units.
No. Supply shifts left 40 units at a common rate, while equilibrium investment falls only 20 units.
Yes. The 20-unit equilibrium decline is the supply shift because investment demand stays fixed.
No. The 40-unit horizontal difference is an investment-demand shift rather than a saving change.
43261.feedback: At rate 8%, S0 supplies 120 and S1 supplies 80, a 40-unit shift. A to B changes equilibrium quantity from 100 to 80. The higher rate induces movement along the schedules, so the equilibrium decline is not the fixed-rate shift.

43290.q: A larger deficit causes the shift shown in saving supply. How should the resulting change in firms' investment from A to B be interpreted?
options: Investment falls 80 units as firms move along D0 in response to the higher real rate.
Investment falls 40 units because the higher real rate shifts the entire investment-demand curve left.
Investment falls 40 units as firms move along D0 in response to the higher real rate.
Investment falls 40 units because the deficit directly reduces project profitability at every real rate.
43290.feedback: A is at 100 and B at 60, so equilibrium investment falls 40 units. D0 remains fixed: the saving contraction raises the real rate from 6% to 8%, making fewer projects worthwhile along the existing demand schedule.

43257.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion, and the lines are straight. A fiscal change lowers public saving by $55 billion at every real rate, while a separate incentive raises planned private saving by $15 billion at every rate. Investment demand does not shift. Which comparison correctly connects the policy shifts with A and B?
options: Saving supply shifts left $40 billion, while investment falls $30 billion; the higher rate induces some additional saving.
Saving supply shifts left $40 billion, while investment falls $20 billion; the higher rate induces some additional saving.
Saving supply shifts left $40 billion and investment falls $20 billion; the remaining $20 billion is a rightward shift of investment demand.
Saving supply shifts left $20 billion and investment falls $40 billion; the equilibrium change measures the fixed-rate supply shift.
43257.feedback: At any given rate, the saving-supply change is −55 + 15 = −$40 billion, matching the horizontal distance between S0 and S1. The marked equilibria move from 100 to 80, so investment falls by $20 billion. The higher rate partly offsets the supply reduction by inducing additional saving along the shifted schedule.

43259.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion. The straight S0 and S1 curves capture a fiscal change, with the private-saving schedule unchanged and D0 fixed. Starting from B, a second policy raises planned private saving by $15 billion at every real rate. How much must public saving rise from its level at B to restore A?
options: $45 billion; together with the $15 billion private-saving increase, this restores a 60-unit supply shortfall.
$5 billion; adding the $15 billion private increase to the 20-unit equilibrium gap restores the original supply schedule.
$55 billion; the private-saving increase must be added to, rather than deducted from, the 40-unit shortfall.
$25 billion; together with the $15 billion private-saving increase, this restores the 40-unit supply shortfall.
43259.feedback: At any given rate, S1 lies 40 units left of S0. Restoring S0 therefore requires $40 billion of additional planned national saving, not merely the 20-unit difference in equilibrium quantity. Private saving supplies $15 billion of that shift, leaving $25 billion of public saving. With D0 fixed, restoring S0 restores A.

43269.q: Saving behavior is unchanged as the market moves from A to B. Which economic change is consistent with the pattern shown?
options: Lower expected project profitability reduces investment demand at each real rate.
Higher expected project profitability increases investment demand at each real rate.
The higher real rate itself shifts investment demand right rather than causing movement along it.
A larger public deficit shifts saving supply left while investment demand stays fixed.
43269.feedback: Both the rate and quantity rise on unchanged S0, with D1 right of D0. Greater project profitability can shift investment demand. A higher rate is part of the equilibrium response, not the cause of a demand shift.

43275.q: With saving behavior unchanged, what could explain the move from A to B?
options: Firms expect stronger future sales, increasing planned investment at each real rate.
The lower real rate itself reduces planned investment at every real rate.
Households become more willing to save, shifting the supply of funds right.
Firms expect weaker future sales, reducing planned investment at each real rate.
43275.feedback: B has a lower rate and smaller quantity on unchanged S0. D1 is left of D0, consistent with weaker expected sales. Lower borrowing costs alone would move along investment demand rather than shifting it.

43270.q: How does the investment-demand change shown affect the equilibrium, and what induces savers to provide the new quantity?
options: The rate rises from 5% to 6% and quantity rises from 80 to 100; the higher return induces movement along S0.
The rate rises from 5% to 7% and quantity rises from 80 to 120 because the rate increase shifts S0 right.
The rate rises from 5% to 7% and quantity rises from 80 to 120; the higher return induces movement along S0.
Quantity rises from 80 to 120 while the rate falls, because stronger investment demand reduces borrowing costs.
43270.feedback: The graph shows A at 80/5 and B at 120/7. Investment demand shifts right, and the higher real rate encourages additional saving along the unchanged supply schedule.

43276.q: If firms reduce investment demand at every real interest rate while saving supply is unchanged, what happens to the equilibrium real rate and quantity of loanable funds?
options: Both the real rate and quantity fall.
Both the real rate and quantity rise.
The real rate rises and quantity falls.
The real rate falls and quantity rises.
43276.feedback: A leftward investment-demand shift lowers both the real rate and equilibrium quantity on an upward-sloping saving-supply curve.

43288.q: National saving falls at every real interest rate while investment demand is unchanged. What happens in the loanable-funds market?
options: The real interest rate rises and equilibrium investment falls.
The real interest rate falls and equilibrium investment rises.
Both the real interest rate and investment rise.
Both the real interest rate and investment fall.
43288.feedback: Lower saving shifts supply left. The real rate rises, and firms reduce investment along the unchanged demand curve.

43272.q: Which change could account for D0 moving to D1?
options: New technology raises expected profitability of investment projects.
A weaker sales outlook reduces expected profitability of investment projects.
Households decide to save more at every real interest rate.
A larger government surplus increases public saving.
43272.feedback: D1 is right of D0, showing stronger demand for investment funds at each rate. Higher expected project returns can explain that shift; household and public saving affect supply.

43273.q: The graph shows the investment-demand response to new technology. Suppose a deficit also reduces saving supply by an unknown amount. Which statement separates the plotted result from that added scenario?
options: The graph alone raises quantity from 80 to 140; with the added saving decline, the net quantity change from 80 is uncertain.
The graph alone raises quantity from 80 to 120; with the added saving decline, the net quantity change from 80 is uncertain.
The graph alone raises quantity from 80 to 120; the extra deficit leaves that final quantity unchanged because both shocks raise the rate.
The graph alone raises quantity from 80 to 120; the extra deficit must reduce quantity below 80 regardless of its size.
43273.feedback: A/B give the demand-only quantity response 80 to 120 on fixed supply. A saving decline shifts supply left, adding upward rate pressure but opposing the demand-driven quantity increase. Its unknown size prevents determining the combined quantity relative to 80.

43287.q: A government deficit increases by $30 billion while planned private saving rises by $10 billion at each real interest rate. With investment demand unchanged, how does the net saving change affect the loanable-funds market?
options: National saving rises $40 billion, shifting supply right; a lower rate raises investment.
National saving falls $20 billion, shifting investment demand left and lowering the rate.
National saving is unchanged because an increase in private saving fully offsets any deficit.
National saving falls $20 billion, shifting supply left; a higher rate crowds out investment.
43287.feedback: Public saving falls $30 billion while private saving rises $10 billion, reducing national saving by $20 billion at a given rate. Supply shifts left; the real rate rises and investment falls along unchanged demand.

43293.q: Planned private saving rises by $30 billion and public saving falls by $10 billion at each real rate. What happens to investment in the loanable-funds model if investment demand is unchanged?
options: Lower national saving raises the real rate and reduces investment along the existing demand curve.
Higher national saving lowers the real rate and raises investment along the existing demand curve.
The $20 billion net saving increase shifts investment demand right and raises the real rate.
Investment is unchanged because opposing saving changes must cancel completely.
43293.feedback: The net national-saving increase is $20 billion at a given rate. Supply shifts right, lowering the real rate and encouraging investment along its unchanged demand curve.

43295.q: A budget improvement raises planned public saving by $25 billion while private saving falls by $10 billion at each real rate. An analyst says this directly raises firms' investment demand. How should that claim be corrected?
options: National saving rises $15 billion; investment demand shifts right because all additional saving is a new project.
National saving falls $35 billion; supply shifts left and investment falls.
National saving is unchanged; any change in public saving is canceled by private saving.
National saving rises $15 billion; supply shifts right, and the lower rate induces investment along unchanged demand.
43295.feedback: National saving rises by $15 billion at each rate, shifting supply right. The lower equilibrium real rate then increases investment along unchanged demand. A saving increase does not itself raise project profitability at every rate.

43289.q: Which fiscal change is consistent with the move from S0 to S1, holding other saving determinants fixed?
options: A larger surplus increases public and national saving.
A larger deficit reduces public and national saving.
An investment tax credit raises the profitability of private projects.
The higher equilibrium rate by itself shifts the entire saving curve left.
43289.feedback: S1 is left of S0, so saving supplied at each real rate falls. A larger government deficit can create that shift. The rate increase is a response to the contraction, not a shift determinant.

43292.q: Which explanation of the move from A to B illustrates the effect of saving on private investment?
options: Lower saving raises borrowing costs, reducing investment along the existing demand curve.
Higher saving lowers borrowing costs, increasing investment along the existing demand curve.
Lower saving raises borrowing costs, shifting the investment-demand curve left.
Lower saving reduces borrowing costs, so firms undertake more investment projects.
43292.feedback: S1 lies left of S0, and B has a higher real rate and less investment than A. The rate increase crowds out investment along the unchanged demand curve.

43297.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion, and the curves are straight. A budget improvement shifts S0 to S1; the private-saving schedule and investment demand are unchanged. What does the graph imply about the rise in public saving and the induced change in private saving between A and B?
options: Public saving rises $60 billion; lower rates induce a $20 billion decline in private saving.
Public saving rises $80 billion; lower rates induce a $40 billion decline in private saving.
Public saving rises $80 billion; the fixed private-saving schedule means private saving cannot change.
Public saving rises $40 billion; the equilibrium investment increase directly measures the policy-induced supply shift.
43297.feedback: The horizontal supply shift is 80 units: at an 8 percent rate S0 is at 60 and S1 is at 140. With the private-saving schedule unchanged, that shift is the $80 billion public-saving increase. Final national saving and investment rise only from 60 to 100, or $40 billion. Private saving consequently changes by 40 − 80 = −$40 billion through movement along its schedule as the rate falls.

43305.q: Both saving supply and investment demand increase. Which statement distinguishes the general prediction from the outcome at A and B?
options: Quantity must rise; the rate is generally ambiguous, and the plotted rate rises.
Quantity must rise; the rate is generally ambiguous, but the plotted rate is unchanged.
Quantity rises and the rate is unchanged; every pair of rightward saving and investment shifts has that rate result.
Quantity is generally ambiguous; the unchanged plotted rate means national saving did not rise.
43305.feedback: Both shifts raise quantity, but they exert opposing pressures on the rate. A and B are both at 6%, so those pressures offset in this drawing. That particular offset is not a universal rule.

43309.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion, and the straight-line shifts summarize all changes in saving and investment behavior. Public saving falls by $10 billion at every real rate, while technology raises investment demand. What private-saving shift is required to reconcile the graph with that fiscal change?
options: Private saving must rise $70 billion: together with public saving falling $10 billion, this gives a $60 billion supply increase.
Private saving must rise $50 billion: together with public saving falling $10 billion, this gives the plotted $40 billion supply increase.
Private saving must rise $30 billion: subtract the $10 billion public-saving loss from the plotted $40 billion increase.
Private saving must rise $10 billion: an unchanged equilibrium rate implies no national-saving change.
43309.feedback: At 6 percent, S0 and D0 each have quantity 40, while S1 and D1 each have quantity 80. Each schedule shifts right by $40 billion. Since national saving combines private and public saving, the private shift must satisfy private change − 10 = 40, giving +$50 billion. The two shifts leave the depicted equilibrium rate at 6 percent.

43311.q: Which pair of events could produce the changes from the solid to the dashed curves?
options: Households plan less saving, and firms expect investment projects to be less profitable.
Households plan more saving, while firms expect investment projects to be less profitable.
The higher quantity itself shifts both schedules, without any change in saving or investment plans.
Households plan more saving, and firms expect investment projects to be more profitable.
43311.feedback: S1 is right of S0 and D1 is right of D0. Higher planned saving explains the supply shift, while higher expected project returns explain investment demand. Equilibrium quantity is a result, not a determinant that shifts both curves.

43313.q: What can the marked new equilibrium tell us that the directions of the two shifts alone cannot?
options: The real rate is 8%; this is the particular result of the relative supply and demand shifts drawn.
The real rate is 6%; this is the particular result of the relative supply and demand shifts drawn.
The real rate is 6%; every simultaneous rightward supply and demand shift must leave rates unchanged.
The real rate is 6%; the quantity increase proves that only saving supply changed.
43313.feedback: B is at 6%, the same rate as A. Theory alone leaves the rate effect of the two increases ambiguous; their actual sizes and slopes in this figure locate the new intersection.

43314.q: The market changes from A to B after saving and investment plans both change. What explains the interest-rate outcome shown?
options: Investment demand dominates here, raising the rate to 8%; different relative shifts could change the rate.
The rate stays at 6% because every equal-direction pair of supply and demand shifts leaves the rate fixed.
The opposing pressures offset here, leaving the rate at 6%; different relative shifts could change the rate.
The rate stays at 6% because a doubling of quantity prevents any change in the price of loanable funds.
43314.feedback: Both marked equilibria are at 6%, though quantity rises from 40 to 80. Greater saving puts downward pressure on the rate and greater investment demand puts upward pressure on it. Their offset is specific to the drawn shifts.

PG5-PC-H-016.q: Consumer spending unexpectedly strengthens while expectations, supply conditions and the natural rate remain unchanged. How does A to B represent the short-run response?
options: Unemployment becomes 1 point below natural and inflation rises 2 points; this is movement along the existing SRPC.
Unemployment becomes 2 points below natural and inflation rises 1 point because LRPC shifts left.
Unemployment becomes 2 points below natural and inflation rises 1 point because expectations immediately shift SRPC upward.
Unemployment becomes 2 points below natural and inflation rises 1 point; this is movement along the existing SRPC.
PG5-PC-H-016.feedback: A is (5,2.5) and B is (3,3.5). A demand change with expectations and supply fixed moves along SRPC0. Compare the unemployment coordinate with LRPC at 5, and compare inflation with A; the cyclical gap does not move natural unemployment.

PG5-PC-H-022.q: An unexpected fall in investment occurs before expectations adjust. Supply conditions and the natural rate are unchanged. What does the plotted move from A to B imply?
options: Unemployment is 1 point above natural and inflation is 2 points lower; demand weakness moves the economy along SRPC0.
Unemployment is 2 points above natural and inflation is 1 point lower; demand weakness moves the economy along SRPC0.
Unemployment is 2 points above natural and inflation is 1 point lower; the change establishes a permanent rise in structural unemployment.
Unemployment is 2 points above natural and inflation is 1 point lower; lower expected inflation has already shifted SRPC0 downward.
PG5-PC-H-022.feedback: A is (5,2.5) and B is (7,1.5). A demand change with expectations and supply fixed moves along SRPC0. Compare the unemployment coordinate with LRPC at 5, and compare inflation with A; the cyclical gap does not move natural unemployment.

PG5-PC-L-018.q: Refer to the graph with A and B on SRPC0. Initially expected inflation is the inflation rate at A, and the economy is at B. Next period expected inflation equals this period’s actual inflation. Hold the natural rate and supply conditions fixed; each one-point expectations change shifts the SRPC vertically by one point with slope unchanged. Compare keeping unemployment at B’s rate with instead keeping actual inflation at B’s current rate. Which next-period outcome follows?
options: Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 5.5%; holding inflation at 4% instead returns unemployment to 5%.
Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 4.5%; holding inflation at 3.5% instead returns unemployment to 5%.
Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 3.5%; expected inflation cannot alter a point already reached.
Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 4.5%; holding inflation at 3.5% instead permanently lowers the natural rate to 3%.
PG5-PC-L-018.feedback: Expectations rise from 2.5 to 3.5, shifting the curve up one point. At unemployment 3, inflation therefore rises from 3.5 to 4.5. Alternatively, actual inflation equal to the new expectation gives natural unemployment at 5. A fixed unemployment target and a fixed inflation target are different continuations.

PG5-PC-X-017.q: Suppose actual inflation is held at B's rate while expectations adjust to it. With supply conditions and the natural rate unchanged, what adjustment does this graph predict?
options: SRPC shifts upward, and unemployment returns to the natural rate of 5%.
SRPC shifts downward, and unemployment returns to the natural rate of 5%.
SRPC shifts upward, permanently raising the natural rate from 3% to 5%.
LRPC shifts left, allowing unemployment to remain at B's 3% once expectations catch up.
PG5-PC-X-017.feedback: B is above A's inflation rate and left of LRPC. Expectations catch up to the higher actual rate, shifting SRPC upward. At that sustained inflation, unemployment returns to the unchanged natural rate 5%.

PG5-PC-X-023.q: Actual inflation is held at B's rate while expectations gradually adjust to it. With the natural rate and supply conditions unchanged, which long-run adjustment fits the figure?
options: SRPC shifts upward, and unemployment returns from 3% toward 5%.
SRPC shifts downward, permanently reducing the natural rate from 7% to 5%.
SRPC shifts downward, and unemployment returns from 7% toward 5%.
LRPC shifts right to 7%, making the demand-induced unemployment increase permanent.
PG5-PC-X-023.feedback: B has unemployment 7 and inflation 1.5, compared with A at natural unemployment 5 and inflation 2.5. Adapting to lower inflation shifts SRPC down; the eventual return to 5 does not change the natural rate.

PG5-PC-M-021.q: How should the change from A to B be interpreted?
options: A movement along SRPC0 consistent with weaker demand while expected inflation is unchanged.
A movement along SRPC0 consistent with stronger demand while expected inflation is unchanged.
A downward shift of SRPC0 caused by lower expected inflation.
A rightward shift of LRPC caused by a permanent increase in structural unemployment.
PG5-PC-M-021.feedback: A and B lie on the same downward-sloping SRPC0, with B showing higher unemployment and lower inflation. That is a demand-related movement along a fixed short-run relationship, not evidence of changed expectations or natural unemployment.

ECON-SP-ELITE-348.q: Why is it a mistake to treat point a as a permanent outcome when actual inflation stays at its displayed rate and the natural rate is unchanged?
options: a lies below natural unemployment; expectations catch up and move the economy toward b on the same inflation line.
a lies above natural unemployment; expectations fall and move the economy toward c on the same inflation line.
a lies below natural unemployment; reaching it permanently shifts LRPC left to U1.
a lies below natural unemployment; the return toward b occurs because the natural rate rises from U1 to U2.
ECON-SP-ELITE-348.feedback: a is left of LRPC at U2 and at inflation I2. As I2 becomes expected, the short-run curve shifts up and the fixed-inflation outcome approaches b. The initial departure from natural unemployment is temporary.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9007.q: Starting at c, policymakers use repeated demand expansion to keep unemployment at U1. Which graph-based criticism applies if they also promise to hold inflation at I2?
options: At I2, adjusted expectations support b at U2, so maintaining U1 instead requires further inflation surprises.
At I2, adjusted expectations support d at U3, so maintaining U1 instead requires further inflation surprises.
At I2, adjusted expectations support b at U2, proving that demand expansion raised natural unemployment.
At I2, point a remains sustainable because keeping actual inflation fixed prevents expectations from changing.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9007.feedback: The graph puts the natural rate at U2 and b at I2. a at U1 is on the old expectations curve. Once expectations adjust, holding U1 below natural requires renewed surprises rather than the original fixed inflation rate.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9046.q: After c to a, policymakers keep actual inflation at its new rate and assume unemployment will stay at a. With unchanged supply conditions, what is the likely correction as expectations adapt?
options: The economy approaches b on LRPC as higher expected inflation shifts SRPC upward.
The economy approaches d on LRPC as higher expected inflation shifts SRPC upward.
The economy approaches b because the natural rate rises to match the earlier demand expansion.
The economy stays at a because demand expansion permanently lowers natural unemployment.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9046.feedback: At the sustained inflation I2, b lies on LRPC and a does not. Expectations catch up, moving the short-run relationship upward and returning unemployment to U2. The natural rate does not change.

ECON-SP-ELITE-351.q: With supply conditions and expectations unchanged, what does the move from c to b on SRPC1 represent?
options: Stronger demand: actual inflation rises while unemployment falls.
Weaker demand: actual inflation falls while unemployment rises.
Higher expected inflation: actual inflation rises at unchanged unemployment.
Lower natural unemployment: LRPC shifts left as the economy moves along SRPC1.
ECON-SP-ELITE-351.feedback: b is above and left of c on the same short-run curve. That movement represents higher actual inflation and lower unemployment with the curve's expectations held fixed.

PM2B3-SRC-FB-004.q: Capital deepening initially raises output per worker with technology and other productivity determinants unchanged. Later, output per worker rises again even though capital per worker is fixed. How do the two increases differ?
options: Both are movements along the same curve caused solely by more capital per worker.
The first is capital deepening; the later gain requires an improvement in another productive factor or technology.
The first is a technology improvement; the later gain is diminishing returns to unchanged capital.
Both show that a falling marginal product causes the level of productivity to fall.
PM2B3-SRC-FB-004.feedback: The first change is a movement along a production relationship as capital per worker rises. The later gain at unchanged capital requires another determinant, such as technology or human capital, to improve.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9038.q: Starting at AD1-AS2, demand moves to AD2 and supply to AS1. An analyst generalizes the plotted output outcome to every demand expansion combined with a supply contraction. What is wrong with that claim?
options: Output is unchanged at Y1 here, but that requires the two output effects to offset; a different-sized pair need not do so.
Output rises to Y2 here, but that requires the demand effect to dominate; a different-sized pair need not do so.
Output is unchanged at Y1 here, proving that opposite-direction AD and SRAS shifts always cancel in output.
Output is unchanged at Y1 here because neither shift can affect real output, only prices.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9038.feedback: The initial and final intersections both have output Y1, while prices rise P1 toP 3. AD expansion raises output and SRAS contraction lowers it; their equality is a feature of these plotted magnitudes, not a universal theorem.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9039.q: The economy moves from AD2-AS1 to AD1-AS2. Compared with reducing AD alone while holding AS1 fixed, what does the simultaneous supply improvement accomplish?
options: It prevents the fall from Y1 to Y3 and leaves output at Y1, while prices fall farther to P1.
It prevents the fall from Y2 to Y1 and leaves output at Y2, while prices fall farther to P2.
It leaves output at Y1 because demand contraction has no real effect even without the supply improvement.
It leaves output at Y1 by shifting aggregate demand back to AD2, reversing the original demand restraint.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9039.feedback: AD restraint alone reaches AD1-AS1 at Y3/P2. Adding the AS2 improvement instead gives AD1-AS2 at Y1/P1. The supply gain offsets the demand-related output loss while reinforcing the price decline.

ECON-SP-ELITE-308.q: Starting at AD1-AS2, AD rises to AD2 and SRAS falls to AS1. Why would using the plotted final output as the effect of the demand expansion alone be misleading?
options: Final output is Y1; the supply contraction offsets the demand-driven increase that would otherwise reach Y2.
Final output is Y2; the supply contraction offsets part of a demand increase that would otherwise reach Y3.
Final output is Y1; that proves the demand expansion has no effect on output even with supply fixed.
Final output is Y1 because the two curves shift in ways that always leave output unchanged regardless of size.
ECON-SP-ELITE-308.feedback: AD2-AS1 is Y1/P3, but demand expansion alone would reach AD2-AS2 at Y2/P2. The unchanged final output combines opposing effects; it does not show an ineffective demand channel.

ECON-SP-ELITE-309.q: Starting at AD2-AS1, AD falls to AD1 while SRAS rises to AS2. Output ends where it began. What does the figure imply about a claim that the supply improvement had no output benefit?
options: The claim is wrong: without the supply improvement, AD1-AS1 would leave output at Y3 rather than Y1.
The claim is wrong: without the supply improvement, AD1-AS1 would leave output at Y2 rather than Y1.
The claim is right: unchanged final output means each individual shock had zero effect on output.
The claim is right: supply improvements affect the price level but cannot affect output in the short run.
